https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Towards a Multiscale Mechanistic Model of Lipid Nanoparticle Formation
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are a versatile drug delivery platform for a wide range of therapeutic modalities including nucleic acids which have received much attention for their use in the COVID-19 vaccines. Modern manufacturing processes for LNPs for nucleic acids involve rapidly mixing an organic stream containing the lipids with an aqueous stream containing the nucleic acids and are conceptually straightforward. However, detailed understanding of LNP formation and structure is still limited and scale-up can be challenging. Mathematical and computational methods are a promising avenue for deepening scientific understanding of the LNP formation process and facilitating improved process development and control. In this presentation, a framework for constructing mechanistic models of reactor-scale and particle-scale processes is first outlined. Initial efforts towards developing a detailed mechanistic model are discussed. In particular, this presentation will focus on two main results: first, the development of advanced thermodynamic models to predictively estimate RNA/lipid solubilities and other important physical properties; and second, the application of phase-field models (PFMs) within a multiscale simulation framework to study the anti-solvent precipitation and RNA encapsulation process. Insights gained from the various models are mapped back to product quality attributes and process insights. Lastly, the use of the models to guide development of advanced process control and optimization strategies is discussed.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Synthesis of Unilammellar Liposomes for Drug Delivery Using Colloidal Packed Bed
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Liposome-based drug delivery systems synthesized using colloidal packed bed technology represent a promising advancement in targeted and efficient therapeutic delivery. We highlight the synthesis and application of liposomes through colloidal packed beds, with particular emphasis on their potential for DNA and RNA delivery as well as the treatment of iron deficiency anemia. The colloidal packed bed uses alumina oxide as packing material within an alumina cylindrical tube sintered at 1100 ºC for 30 minutes. Our synthesis process used one-step drying and hydration of lipid films in the packed bed to form desirable small unilamellar liposomes. Additionally, we can obtain low polydisperse liposomes and load cargoes such as iron and DNA. We also aim to achieve higher encapsulation efficiency of iron using anionic lipids such as 1,2-Dipalmitoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoglycerol, sodium salt (DPPG), and DNA using the cationic lipid 1,2-Dioleoyl-3-trimethylammonium propane (DOTAP), as well as the helper lipid 1,2-di-(9Z-octadecenoyl)-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine (DOPE) and PEGylated lipid (ALC-0159). We aim to adapt our method to accommodate various nucleic acids, including RNA and siRNA, for downstream applications. Synthesized liposomes were measured for size using nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) and dynamic light scattering (DLS), while the bilayer lamellarity was confirmed using a Cryo-Transmission Electron Microscope (Cryo-TEM). The encapsulation technique using a colloidal packed bed aims to provide an alternative to existing techniques, such as microfluidics and the impinging jet mixer, which are currently used for the synthesis of liposome-based drug delivery systems.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Virtual High-Throughput Screening of Transition Metal Mechanophores with Ab Initio Modeling and Machine Learning
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Mechanophores are force-responsive molecules that undergo controlled bond breaking or rearrangement under applied force. Due to their diverse physical and chemical responses to mechanical stimuli, mechanophores broad applications in polymer strengthening, force probing, drug delivery, and waste polymer applications and have been extensively studied in recent years. Neverhtless, the majority of existing mechanophores are organic molecules, and mechanophore design and discovery currently relies on less efficient experimental trial-and-error. Expansion of mechanophore space to transition metal containing mechanophores would allow for even greater tunability of properties, but their synthesis and experimental characterization is more challenging than their organic counterparts. We have thus implemented a workflow for high-throughput computational discovery of transition metal mechanophores. First, we screen the Cambridge Structural Database (CSD) to gather synthetically accessible molecular candidates for two classes of mechanophores: spin-crossover and coordination-switching. Across more than 1,100 candidate complexes, we carry out force-free geometry optimizations using density functional theory (DFT), and we also characterize the force-responsiveness of these mechanophores using simulations that explicitly incorporate external force (i.e., EFEI and CoGEF). From these simulations, we identify key chemical features and construct mechanochemistry-tailored machine learning (ML) models to drastically accelerate computational discovery. To date, we have identified 500+ metal mechanophores with high reactivity, distinct and critical functionalities, and versatile for real-world applications. The 150+ spin-crossover mechanophores, for instance, exhibit force-activated spin-crossover between magnetic states. They are thus compatible for in-situ force-probing and damage detection for the majority of engineering polymers which are opaque, resolving the limitations of current mechanophores which rely on optical signals. The 350+ coordination-switching mechanophores, on the other hand, have mechanochemical reactivity comparable with the most labile mechanophores currently discovered. Their facile responses make them building blocks for ultra-strong polymer networks. Finally, we further identified most promising candidates for follow-up synthesis.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Design of Ion-Sieve for Selective Adsorption of Lithium from Geothermal Brine
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: The growing demand for lithium-ion batteries necessitates efficient and sustainable lithium extraction technologies. Geothermal brines provide an alternative lithium source; however, their complex ionic composition challenges selective lithium recovery. Hydrogen manganese oxides (H 4 Mn 4.5 O 12 ) are widely studied as lithium-ion sieves due to their high selectivity for lithium ions. Still, its structural instability and manganese dissolution during adsorption-desorption cycles limit long-term performance. This study introduced zirconium (Zr) doping into the spinel-type Li 4 Mn 5 O 12 precursor through a one-step calcination process (450 °C for 24 hours at 10 °C min −1 ), ensuring an energy-efficient synthesis process of Li 4 Mn 4.5 Zr 0.5 O 12 (LMZO) matrix. The resulting spinel H 4 Mn 4.5 Zr 0.5 O 12 (HMZO), after acid activation, underwent comprehensive characterization employing several analytical techniques, including Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) surface area, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS). The HMZO exhibited a lithium adsorption capacity of 26.81 mg/g in synthetic brine, with a maximum capacity of 35 mg/g at an adsorbent-to-solution ratio of 0.017 g/50 mL, while restricting manganese dissolution to 0.78% after five adsorption-desorption cycles. Adsorption kinetics followed the pseudo-second-order model, while the Freundlich isotherm indicated a heterogeneous Li-H ion exchange mechanism. The thermodynamic analysis confirmed that lithium adsorption was endothermic and entropy-driven, improving with increased temperature. These findings highlight the enhanced stability and reusability of HMZO, demonstrating its potential as a next-generation lithium-ion sieve for sustainable lithium recovery from geothermal brines. Further optimization, including refining zirconium content and activation conditions, is necessary to maximize long-term adsorption performance.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Integrated Process Design of Passage Culture and Freezing for Mesenchymal Stem Cells Toward Establishment of Working Cell Banks
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are one of the most promising sources in the field of regenerative medicine such as due to their multipotency and immunosuppression. The cells are widely used in preclinical and clinical regenerative medicine including the treatment of acute graft versus host diseases, type I diabetes mellitus, and chronic liver disease. In MSC manufacturing, cell bank systems are generally accepted as the most practical approach, which consists of two types of cell banks: master cell banks and working cell banks. Master cell banks are developed for the preservation of specific cell lines, while working cell banks store cells that can be used for product manufacturing. For establishment of working cell banks for MSCs, the passage culture and freezing processes are at the core of the cell bank, although there are no clear standards for the design of working cell banks. Hence, working cell banks for MSCs have been designed empirically 1 . In the field of process systems engineering, several regenerative medicine-related processes have been explored by model-based approaches, e.g., cultivation of MSCs 2 and batch freezing of induced pluripotent stem cells 3 . However, these models were limited to unit operations, and it has been difficult to design working cell banks for MSCs with the previously developed models. In this work, an integrated process model of passage culture and freezing for MSCs was newly developed to design the entire passage culture and freezing processes toward establishment of working cell banks for the cells. From a process modeling perspective, it is necessary to consider the impact of the passage culture process on the freezing process. Therefore, we adopted the cell diameter as the connecting variable between the two processes. The cell diameter was expressed as a function of the cumulative population doubling level in the passage culture process model, and the freezing process model calculated the cell survival rate and the number of living cells after thawing using the cell diameter as the input. Given the number of passage operations, the days per passage, and the cooling rate of the freezer, the integrated process model can evaluate the cumulative population doubling level, the cell survival rate, and the number of living cells after thawing. The application of the developed model was demonstrated in a case study. As a result, a feasible parameter range of working cell banks for MSCs was obtained, given a set of constraints which consisted of the cumulative population doubling level, the cell survival rate, and the number of living cells after thawing. These results would be useful for designing working cell banks for MSCs. In the ongoing work, we are conducting probabilistic simulations to obtain a feasible parameter range of working cell banks for MSCs considering uncertainty. References 1. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Biophysical Engineering of Cytotoxic T Lymphocytes Via Contact-Dependent Phosphatase Exclusion Using Micropatches
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Despite decades of innovation in cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL)–based therapies, their efficacy in solid tumors remains limited compared to the remarkable success of CAR T cells in hematologic malignancies. A key barrier is the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, which restricts CTL accessibility and rapidly diminishes their effector function, often within hours of infusion, even in cells primed ex vivo with robust cytotoxic and proliferative capacity. Therefore, strategies that sustain CTL functionality post-transfer are of interest to increase their therapeutic potential in solid tumors. Here, we present a novel cell-surface engineering approach leveraging contact-driven CD45-phosphatase exclusion, a biomaterial-based strategy that modulates CTL phenotype and sustains their functionality post-infusion. We engineered micron-scale polymeric micropatches fabricated from either polylactic-co-glycolide (PLGA) or hyaluronic acid (HA), both biopolymers with demonstrated clinical compatibility. These micropatches bind efficiently to CTLs, and, upon contact, induce spatial exclusion of CD45 phosphatase at the CTL contact interface. This exclusion was validated through diffusion-signaling-based mathematical modeling and high-resolution imaging, establishing it as a biochemical mechanism for tonic CTL stimulation, an effect that conventional nanoparticle configurations failed to achieve. Notably, this stimulation was observed to occur independent of the specific material used or receptor engaged, suggesting a platform-agnostic mechanism driven solely by contact-mediated reorganization at the CTL surface. We focused on PLGA-based micropatches, termed PMPEs (Polymeric Micropatches for Phosphatase Exclusion), and demonstrated through bulk RNA sequencing that PMPE modification induces transcriptomic changes consistent with enhanced CTL effector potential. A comprehensive array of in vitro assays, including ELISA, calcium flux, immunofluorescence, proliferation, and cytotoxicity, alongside in vivo studies (biodistribution, immunophenotyping, pathology), revealed that PMPE-CTLs exhibit enhanced persistence, robust Type 1 immunostimulatory response, and excellent tolerability. In aggressive B16F10 melanoma models, PMPE-CTLs significantly improved tumor control, with 50% survival beyond 25 days, compared to no survival in unmodified CTLs. When combined with systemic IL-15 superagonist (IL15sa) therapy, PMPE-CTLs extended survival beyond 35 days in 46% of mice, with 15.4% achieving complete remission, a result not observed in the IL15sa + CTL group alone. Altogether, this work introduces a contact-driven cell engineering strategy as a simple, scalable, and drug-free biomaterial-based approach to modulate CTL behavior and sustain their functionality within hostile tumor microenvironments. Remarkably, this effect is achieved even with blank microparticles, without the need for conventional drug loading. The platform is readily compatible with existing clinical manufacturing workflows, offering a simple yet effective avenue for advancing the development of next-generation CTL therapies for solid tumor management.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Machine Learning-Enabled Self-Driving Laboratory for Accelerated Emulsifiable Concentrates Design
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Crop protection formulations are essential for improving crop yields to sustain a growing population. However, formulation design and development remain primarily empirical, often requiring up to a year to design a formulation product. While principal rules and empirical methods such as the hydrophilic-lipophilic balance (HLB) theory, are effective in control experiments, they struggle to investigate optimal candidate materials for industrial applications. Hence, the development of agrochemical formulation heavily relies on an extensive number of experiments. To accelerate the formulation design process, we will present our level-4 self-driving laboratory (SDL) system for formulation development, powered by machine learning models based on past experimental data. As a level-4 SDL, chemists will design the search space and the SDL will conduct closed-loop experiments which are formed by multiple tasks. This system autonomously designs, conducts, characterises, and refines experiments iteratively. By significantly reducing the workload of formulation scientists, our SDL enhances efficiency and accelerates innovation in crop protection formulation.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: AI-Powered Materials Discovery and Design: A Computational Framework for Tailoring Microstructural Properties
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Inverse design remains a central challenge in materials engineering, where optimizing microstructures to achieve targeted properties is often computationally prohibitive. Traditional methods struggle with inverting structure-property relationships due to the high dimensionality and stochastic complexity of microstructures. To overcome these challenges, we introduce PoreFlow , a data-driven computational framework that leverages continuous normalizing flows (CNFs) for high-throughput microstructure generation. Unlike conventional generative models, PoreFlow embeds target properties directly into the latent space, enabling precise and efficient inverse design. We demonstrate the power of this approach through the generation of 3D porous microstructures, where our model consistently achieves R2 scores above 91.5% for reconstruction and greater than 92% for new sample generation. Compared to GAN-based models, which often face instability and mode collapse, PoreFlow offers a robust, stable training process and enhanced interpretability. Its modular architecture also allows for extensions beyond image-based design representations by modifying the autoencoder component. This work has broad implications for materials discovery and design in various applications such as energy storage, catalysis, and beyond, providing a scalable and interpretable method for engineering microstructures with tailored properties. By integrating machine learning and materials informatics, PoreFlow advances inverse design, making it faster, more reliable, and more accessible to researchers and engineers.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Transfer Learning from Batch to Continuous Line for Pharmaceutical Tablet Production
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: In the pharmaceutical industry, the manufacturing site, scale, and equipment for a drug product can be changed in the development and commercial production stages, considering the change in demand for clinical trial materials and commercial products. During the early phase of these changes, experimental data are scarce in the new condition, which makes it challenging to build a reliable model using conventional machine learning (ML) approaches. An effective ML technique to tackle the situation with limited data is transfer learning (TL). TL can improve the prediction performance of a model for one domain, i.e., target domain (TD), by transferring knowledge from a related domain, i.e., source domain (SD). Previous research successfully applied TL to pharmaceutical manufacturing process scale-up for roller compaction [1], spray-drying [2], and tableting [3]. However, further investigations are still needed to stimulate TL implementation in the pharmaceutical industry. For example, TL’s applicability has yet to be investigated when a production line with several unit processes is changed to a new one with different unit processes. No previous research has revealed the impact of input variables, including process parameters (PP) and material attributes (MA) of intermediate products, on the TL model’s prediction accuracy for critical quality attributes (CQA). This study aims to clarify TL’s applicability to the transition of a pharmaceutical tablet production line from batch to continuous and evaluate the effect of PP and MA as input variables on CQA prediction accuracy, comparing TL with two conventional ML approaches. This study adopted frustratingly easy heterogeneous domain adaption (FEHDA) [4] as a TL algorithm. FEHDA creates three feature spaces from input variables: 1) common to both SD and TD, 2) unique to SD, and 3) unique to TD. One conventional ML approach is ‘SD+TD’ where a model is constructed using input variables common to SD and TD. The other is ‘TD’ where only TD data are available for model-building. A schematic diagram in the attached image illustrates the matrix structure differences between the three model-building methods. The batch line (BL) and continuous line (CL) were regarded as SD and TD, respectively. BL involves high-shear wet granulation, fluidized bed drying, screening, lubrication blending, and tableting. On the other hand, CL consists of twin screw wet granulation, fluidized bed drying, screening, lubrication blending, and tableting. Since the screening and tableting equipment in BL and CL has the same design and operating principles, the PP of two processes were regarded as input variables common to both domains. In contrast, the PP of the remaining processes in BL and CL were regarded as input variables unique to SD and TD, respectively. MA and lubricant ratio were regarded as input variables common to both domains because they were measured using the same method. The dissolution rate at 15 min (%), a CQA of the final product, was measured as an output variable. Fifteen BL lots and five CL lots were prepared as SD and TD training data to build Gaussian process regression (GPR) [5] models. The GPR model’s prediction performance was evaluated using TD test data of eleven CL lots, which was not included in TD training data. Six GPR models were constructed using two types of input variables, i.e., PP and PP+MA, and three kinds of model-building methods, i.e., TL, SD+TD, and TD. Besides, six TD training/test data combinations were prepared to evaluate the GPR model’s robustness by root mean square error of prediction (RMSEP). A bar chart in the attached image shows the mean and standard deviation values of RMSEP for the six GPR models. When using only PP as input variables, the TL model achieved the smallest RMSEP value of 3.6%, compared to the RMSEP values of 5.1% and 5.8% in the SD+TD and TD models, respectively. While the SD+TD model used only PP that are common to both domains, the TL model employed not only PP common to both domains but also PP unique to each domain, which contributed to improving the prediction performance of the TL model. In addition, the TL model with only PP achieved the RMSEP value of 3.6% without using MA as input variables, which was comparable to the RMSEP values of 3.5% and 3.3% in the TL and SD+TD models with PP+MA. Using MA as input variables common to both domains improved the RMSEP value of the SD+TD model, because MA potentially correlate with CQA, and their relationship is independent of manufacturing equipment. Regardless of input variable types, the TD models were not robust and showed the worst RMSEP values due to the scarcity of TD training data. This study concludes that TL can improve prediction accuracy even when MA data are not available. Consequently, TL holds the potential to streamline process development activities by reducing the time and cost required for MA data collection. Furthermore, a PP-based TL model could be critical in CQA prediction when intermediate products such as powders and granules cannot be sampled in the containment facilities for highly potent APIs, or manufacturing site is transferred to a contract manufacturing organization. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Molecular Dynamics and Machine Learning for Designing Peptide Probes for Vapor-Phase Sensing to Improve Disease Diagnostics and Monitoring.
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Rapid and non-invasive tests for disease can be crucial for human health, especially during pandemics like COVID-19. Breath analysis hold promise as an approach for disease detection, as the human breath contains volatile organic compounds (VOCs) that vary in balance with the illness. Traditional disease diagnostic tools are often slow, invasive or require travel to a testing site. A preliminary study has validated the concept of developing a biosensor comprising a multiplex of peptide probes capable of binding diseased VOCs for diagnosing diseases. These peptides, ranging from 8 to 20 amino acids, inherit molecular motifs and VOC-binding affinities akin to odorant-binding proteins (OBPs), with additional features for easy immobilization on a transistor surface. The study has demonstrated selective electrical response to a target VOC verses a confounding VOC in a simulated breath flow. However, homology transfer is not flawless, and eliminating binding residues from their native protein structure alters their conformational behavior and exact VOC-binding profile. Methods are needed to fine-tune the sequence of each peptide probe in the sensor design to enhance the specificity of the entire multiplex for targeting diseases. In this project, we aim to develop and verify a high-throughput computational screen for peptide/VOC binding: The project aims to create a physics-based computational screen using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and enhanced sampling methods, such as Metadynamics (MetaD) to predict the binding affinities between peptide probes and VOC molecules. This screen will allow for the exploration of many potential peptide sequences and generate data points for machine learning (ML) modeling. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations will be used both for developing new fundamental understanding (e.g., structure function relationships in peptide/VOC bound states) while also providing key information for training ML models to estimate binding affinity from sequence alone.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Novel Ligand Discovery for Rare Earth Element Separation Using Chemical Language Model and High-Throughput Experiments
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Rare Earth Elements (REEs) are indispensable to modern technologies, including renewable energy, electronics, defense systems, and advanced medical devices. Despite their importance, REE supply chains remain vulnerable to geopolitical tensions and environmental challenges. Additionally, separating individual REEs is difficult due to their similar physicochemical properties and their co-occurrence in deposits. Liquid–liquid extraction (LLE), relying on ligand-metal binding affinity, is the primary industrial method for REE recovery. However, current LLE ligand extractants typically have low binding affinity and separation efficiency towards REE, requiring extensive solvent usage and generating significant waste. Therefore, developing innovative extraction technologies, especially novel ligands with enhanced binding affinity and selectivity towards REEs is essential. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) have shown promise in predicting ligands for REEs but still face key limitations. The lack of publicly available datasets and limited experimental data hinder the development and validation of robust predictive models. Furthermore, existing methods largely focus on prediction rather than ligand design, underscoring the need for innovative approaches capable of designing novel and effective molecules for REE separations. Recently, large language models (LLMs), specifically chemical language models (CLMs), have revolutionized novel molecule design. Pre-trained on billions of molecules, CLMs serve as a powerful framework to enhance the performance of downstream tasks in situations with limited labeled data, paving the way for breakthroughs in REE binding ligands design. In this work, we aim to leverage state-of-the-art AI and ML methods combined with high-throughput experimental techniques to design novel ligands for efficient REE separation. Summarizing data from previous literature, we first fine-tuned pre-trained CLMs to obtain a ligand-REE binding affinity predictor. We then applied this trained predictor to screen a large molecule set and identify novel ligands with potentially enhanced REE binding affinity. These candidate ligands underwent high-throughput experimental validation, significantly increasing available experimental data. This newly validated data was reincorporated into the training dataset, enhancing model accuracy and extrapolative capabilities through an active learning cycle. This iterative cycle of prediction, validation, and refinement continuously improved model performance, ultimately producing a robust REE-binding affinity predictor and facilitating the discovery of novel ligands with superior binding affinity and selectivity.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Similarity-Based Classification of Concentration Profiles in Chemical Reactions to Assist Kinetic Model Development
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: In the fields of reaction engineering and process systems engineering, the development of mechanistic models based on physical and chemical principles has long been a central focus. Within the domain of organic chemistry, kinetic studies play a crucial role in bridging the understanding of reaction mechanisms with the construction of predictive models. Despite their value, the application of kinetic approaches in organic synthesis has historically been limited [1]. This is largely due to the deep domain knowledge and significant manual effort required to analyze and interpret reaction mechanisms for model development. Since around 2005, however, there has been a noticeable increase in research dedicated to kinetic studies of organic reactions [2–5]. In addition, new analytical methodologies have emerged—such as reaction progress kinetic analysis [1, 5, 6] and variable time normalization analysis [7, 8]—which have improved the accessibility of kinetic evaluation. More recently, efforts have been made to incorporate machine learning techniques into kinetic analysis workflows. These include platforms like AI-DARWIN [9] and studies on classifying organic reaction mechanisms using machine learning [10]. Nevertheless, previous studies have primarily focused on specific types of reactions, which limits their general applicability across a broader range of chemical systems. In this study, we propose a data-driven framework that enables automatic classification of chemical reactions based on their time-dependent concentration profiles, thereby facilitating the identification of underlying mechanisms and the construction of corresponding kinetic models. Our approach focuses on extracting similarity among various reactions by comparing their normalized concentration-time data. By identifying the most similar cases from a reference dataset, we aim to identify possible mechanisms and rate laws that govern the unknown reaction under investigation. We confirmed that neural network-based models can effectively capture nonlinear and dynamic features of the reaction profiles. In addition, several similarity evaluation methods will be explored, such as k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN). Once a similar reaction is identified, the system suggests potential kinetic model candidates and fits the model parameters to the observed data. This could enable automatic selection and construction of the most appropriate kinetic representation for the given reaction. [1] D. G. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Dimensional Evolution of Physical Force- and Field-Induced Chirality: From 2D Elastomeric Metasurfaces to 3D Magnetoplasmonic Superstructures and Beyond
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: The ability to dynamically control chiral optical properties is essential for advancing next-generation optoelectronic and photonic applications. In this study, we demonstrate a dimensional evolution in chirality modulation, transitioning from two-dimensional (2D) elastomeric metasurfaces to three-dimensional (3D) plasmonic chiral responses induced by helical magnetic fields. By integrating these approaches, we establish a unified strategy for achieving real-time and reconfigurable chirality control. We first fabricate fingerprint-inspired elastomeric grating metasurfaces (EGMS) using a nanoimprinting method with polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) followed by gold deposition. These metasurfaces exhibit chiral optical responses due to symmetry breaking induced by pattern (P) and curvature (T), which can be actively tuned by adjusting the skew angle (θ). As a 2D chiral system, EGMS provides a robust platform for structural chirality manipulation. Extending this concept into the 3D domain, we explore plasmonic chiral nanostructures influenced by helical magnetic fields. The application of such fields induces a tunable and reversible chiroptical response, enabling precise control over optical activity. This transition from 2D structural chirality to 3D magnetic-field-driven chirality broadens the scope of tunable chiral photonics, demonstrating how external stimuli can dynamically modulate optical properties. By bridging structural and plasmonic chiral modulation across different dimensions, this study establishes a versatile framework for the design of tunable optical filters, sensors, and polarization-dependent devices. The synergy between 2D metasurfaces and 3D magnetic-field-driven chirality provides a new avenue for the development of advanced chiral photonic materials with broad applications in optoelectronics.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Data-Driven Spray Deposition of Self-Assembled Block Copolymer Thin Films: A Scalable Approach for Morphology Control and Mechanistic Insights
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Block copolymer (BCP) thin films are useful for synthesizing functional materials because of their well-known capabilities to self-assemble into organized nanoscale structures. These materials can be utilized in diverse applications, including lithographic nanopatterning, nanoporous membrane fabrication, and nano-catalysis. However, for their widespread implementation there is need for precise control over their nanoscale morphology using scalable and cost-effective deposition methods. Current synthesis approaches usually involve multi-step processes, specialized materials, and equipment, limiting scalability while increasing costs. Spray deposition techniques address these limitations by enabling the coating of non-planar substrates and reducing manufacturing complexity and costs. In this study, we present a data-driven scalable spray-deposition method to fabricate self-assembled, nanostructured thin films with tailored morphologies. By integrating machine learning algorithms, we optimize the precursor composition and spray parameters to achieve well-defined morphologies directly during deposition in a single step, eliminating the need for post-deposition annealing. Using a program-controlled ultrasonic spray system we explored the complex phase map of six poly(styrene-block-2-vinylpyridine) (PS-b-P2VP) diblock copolymer systems, which are deposited onto functionalized silicon wafers. This simple process yielded various nanostructures, including horizontal cylinders, vertical inverse cylinders, vertical lamellae, and hybrid structures. Also, we monitored the structure formation during the drying process using GISAXS and spectroscopic ellipsometry and confirmed the final morphologies with SEM imaging. The in-situ characterization allows better understanding of the morphology formation mechanism. This method provides a rapid, cost-effective, and scalable approach for producing morphology-controlled BCP films on a wide range of substrates, map the morphology phase space and provide mechanistic insight on the formation process.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Resonance Invariant Graph Representation (RIGR) for Molecular Property Prediction
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Chemical datasets predominantly use SMILES strings to represent molecules, which provide a convenient encoding of Lewis structures by depicting atoms and their bonds, such as single and double bonds. Most machine learning software packages for chemistry, such as chemprop, rely on this SMILES representation as their input. However, this representation depicts only a single resonance structure, even for molecules with multiple resonance forms—common in drug design, organic photovoltaics, and agrochemicals. If a different resonance structure is provided as input, the software may interpret it as a different molecule and produce a different prediction. To overcome this problem, we introduce a Resonance Invariant Graph Representation (RIGR). RIGR is a graph featurizer that inherently ensures resonance invariance by using only resonance invariant atom and bond features in chemprop. By mapping all resonance structures of a molecule to a single graph and discarding resonance-dependent features like bond type, RIGR eliminates the ambiguity in molecular representation. We present a detailed comparison of RIGR's performance against chemprop's native featurizer in predicting the standard heat of formation. We introduce metrics to quantify resonance variance and assess its impact on model predictions. Additionally, we perform Shapley analysis to examine the model's reliance on different atom and bond features, revealing that many features of the native featurizer hold limited relevance in making the final prediction. Using 60% fewer features, the models trained with RIGR show consistent feature importance across different weight initializations, requiring a smaller ensemble of models. While augmenting the data with all resonance structures for training offers a solid solution for implicitly imposing resonance invariance, it introduces significant computational challenges and costs. We also quantify the impact of dataset size, demonstrating that RIGR's performance remains robust, even on smaller datasets. For broader use beyond resonance, RIGR achieves comparable results across chemprop benchmarks for both regression and classification tasks. Building on these promising results, we leverage RIGR to develop a robust, chemistry-informed ML model for predicting gas-phase radical thermochemistry, where resonance plays a significant role. Ultimately, RIGR offers a robust featurizer that enforces resonance invariance while maintaining performance on property prediction tasks and avoids the complexities of generating and augmenting resonance structures. RIGR paves the way for the development of interpretable, chemistry-informed machine learning models.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Screening of Solvents for Capturing PFAS Via a Data Science Approach
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: The development and broad application of single-layer and multilayer (ML) plastics in the food packaging, pharmaceuticals, and cosmetics industries have served various purposes, including ensuring consumer product safety, shelf life, and handling (Barry, 2022). However, the recycling rate for these materials is low, particularly in the US, which only reaches 9% (Geyer et al. 2017). The emergence of solvent-based-physical plastic separation processes, such as the Solvent Targeted Recovery And Precipitation (STRAP™) process, has facilitated the recycling of these plastic wastes that cannot be mechanically recycled, resulting in the heightened recyclability of post-industrial waste plastics (Walker et al. 2020; Zhao et al. 2018). This technology involves the sequential separation of ML plastics into their various polymer constituents over a series of solvent washes, recovering high-quality polymer resins for reuse in food packaging and other consumer products. However, with the emergence of the Chemicals of Concern (Aurisano et al. 2021; Zimmermann et al. 2022) such as Per-and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) that may be non-intentionally introduced (Tumu et al. 2024) into post-consumer waste (PCW) plastics somewhere along the plastic waste management supply chain such as the material recovery facilities, human use, or the environment, current mechanical and solvent-based recycling infrastructures face a significant challenge in ensuring contaminant-free recycled plastics. Moreover, the ubiquitousness of PFAS in the environment and their endocrine-disruptive nature has prompted legislative bans on the industrial use of fluorinated compounds as processing aids, including fluoropolymers across the US, particularly in the food packaging industry, to varying detection limits (Bulawska et al. 2025; Norris et al. 2022; Zheng et al. 2023). Therefore, extending solvent-based plastic recycling infrastructures to remediate short-chain PFAS from PCW plastics is paramount for increasing the recyclability of plastic wastes. However, unlike the finite number of polymers, 15,000 EPA-identified small-molecule PFAS could contaminate PCW plastics (Gaines et al. 2023). Therefore, this study applies data science approaches to quickly identify solvents to capture these PFAS from plastic wastes – ensuring PFAS-free post-consumer recycled plastics. This study expands the STRAP process to incorporate the capture of PFAS using solvents by treating them as an additional layer in selective dissolution. The objective is to identify solvents that selectively dissolve PFAS while preserving other polymers present in the PCW plastics. This approach leverages the partition coefficient (LogD) and the solubility of PFAS in various solvents—predicted via molecular-scale modeling—to identify solvents that facilitate the preferential partitioning of PFAS (LogD > 0) from the polymer matrix into the solvent phase. Specifically, the partition coefficients of each PFAS in different polymers and solvents are essential for evaluating a solvent’s ability to extract PFAS from a given polymer. Additionally, the solubility of each PFAS in different solvents must be assessed to determine the effectiveness of each solvent in capturing PFAS. This molecular-scale modeling involves performing density functional theorem (DFT) calculations on each PFAS to obtain their surface screening charges (i.e., sigma profiles) that necessitate the prediction of relevant molecular properties and the use of the COnductor-like Screening MOdel for Real Solvents (COSMO-RS) software, grounded in quantum chemistry principles, that enables accurate prediction of their LogD and solubilities. However, predicting the LogD of the 15,000 PFAS in 10 different polymers present in PCW plastics in 1000 solvent requires ~15,000,000 molecular simulations or experiments and over 15,000 human hours of simulation time, eliminating the feasibility of experimental screening approaches and requiring significant computational resources. Therefore, PFAS remediation from PCW plastics requires leveraging data science tools for a more efficient PFAS capture strategy. Hypothesizing that structurally similar PFAS have similar molecular properties, this work identifies families of structurally similar PFAS via dimensionality reduction approaches and identifies solvents that can target each family. This approach significantly reduces the number of molecular simulations by 100,000 times and the computational time required. The Molecular ACCess System (MACCS) keys, a one-hot encoding molecular representation, obtained from the open-source rdkit python library, were adopted to represent each PFAS molecule, and t-SNE, a dimensionality reduction technique, was used to transform the structural data from a high-dimensional space to a low-dimensional space for easy visualization. This analysis successfully identified seven distinct families of PFAS having different functional groups and structural features. To test our hypothesis founded on structural similarity, we selected 50 PFAS spanning the entire latent space to perform a pair-wise comparison between their similarity score and LogD magnitude difference. Using polyethylene (PE) as the reference polymer, the LogD values of each PFAS were predicted in five different solvents using the COSMO-RS software. Our results show that 70% similarity is the threshold value for our hypothesis to hold. Therefore, using this threshold value, we performed a guided clustering to determine the number of clusters that would ensure a minimum of 70% structural similarity within each cluster across the entire PFAS latent space. Due to the inherent inability of existing dimensionality techniques, such as t-SNE and UMAP, to perform such guided clustering, a graph-based clustering approach was adopted. Given the 70% threshold value, an undirected graph was developed to represent the interconnectivity between PFAS based on this similarity threshold value (i.e., nodes representing PFAS and edges with at least 70% similarity). While ongoing works involve examining the topology of our undirected graph to identify clusters of interconnected PFAS, our results show that 800 PFAS are structurally unique, having no connection with other PFAS. This result provides insights into PFAS that may be difficult or easy to target via solvent-based approaches. Our results also show that tetrahydrofuran (THF), a biomass-based solvent, proves promising in targeting a wide variety of PFAS from PE. Other ongoing works include applying our solvent screening framework to an existing ML plastic film to identify families of PFAS targeted using selected solvents proposing solvent-based plastic recycling also as a possible pretreatment step for other plastic recycling technologies. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Caffeine Meets Silver: Designing N-Heterocyclic Chalcogenone Ligands for Anticancer Applications through Experimental and DFT Studies
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Caffeine and theophylline are bioactive compounds that can be used as scaffolds to synthesize imidazolium salts that serve as precursors to N-heterocyclic thione (NHT) and selone (NHSe) ligands. These chalcogenone ligands have been used to prepare coordination complexes with a variety of metals, including palladium, platinum, silver, and mercury. In particular, the silver compounds have potential applications as anticancer drugs. This presentation outlines the syntheses, molecular structures, reactivity and DFT calculations of four new N-heterocyclic chalcogenone ligands derived from caffeine or theophylline. More specifically, these novel ligands have been used to prepare several series of silver(I) complexes of general formula [Ag((i)CaffE R ) n ]X (n = 2, 3, 4; R = Me, Bz; E = S, Se; X = NO 3 , BF 4 , ClO 4 ), several of which have been structurally characterized by X-ray crystallography. In order to assess the electronic effect of the pyrimidinedione backbone in the caffeine derivatives, the simpler imidazole-based analogues and their silver complexes have also been isolated and fully characterized. Experimental and computational studies to evaluate and correlate the biological activity of the silver complexes will also be discussed in this presentation.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Early-Stage Conceptual Design and Scale-up Analysis of Continuous Flow Electrosynthesis: A Case Study on Ibuprofen Production Via Electrochemical Carboxylation
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Electrochemical synthesis is emerging as a promising pathway for sustainable pharmaceutical manufacturing, offering a greener alternative to traditional chemical routes. While most electrochemical reactions are developed in batch mode, there is growing interest in translating them into continuous flow systems, which offer advantages such as improved control of reaction conditions, enhanced safety, greater productivity, and easier scalability for industrial implementation. However, early-stage design and scale-up of such systems remain underexplored, particularly for pharmaceutical applications. This study presents a structured framework for the conceptual design and scale-up analysis of continuous flow electrosynthesis processes. The framework integrates scale-up modeling, sensitivity analysis, and simulation-based optimization under uncertainty to support informed early-stage decision-making. To demonstrate the framework's applicability, we apply it to the continuous production of ibuprofen via electrochemical carboxylation, adapting the batch process developed by Mena et al. (2019). In this reaction, 1-chloro-4-isobutylbenzene undergoes carboxylation using CO₂ at a silver cathode in ionic liquids. We model the electrochemical reactor as a steady-state plug flow reactor (PFR) with uniform mass transfer characteristics. To represent industrial stack designs, we implement multiple PFRs in parallel, with each PFR representing a single electrolyte flow channel. It is assumed that these channels are positioned between cathode and anode pairs and are separated by membranes to prevent product crossover. Reactor sizing is guided by commercially available electrode surface areas and standard stack configurations to ensure practical feasibility. Additionally, we model post-electrolysis separation and purification steps to enable full-process analysis. The analysis applies the e-NRTL thermodynamic model to account for electrolyte non-idealities. In alignment with the batch experiments, CO₂ is assumed to be pre-dissolved into the electrolyte before entering the reactor, which justifies treating the system as a single-phase liquid process during electrolysis. We conduct a global sensitivity analysis using the Sobol method to identify the most influential input parameters affecting the performance of the process. These include current density, Faradaic efficiency, flow rate, active electrode area, and electrode spacing, all of which influence conversion, energy consumption, and cost. Although Mena et al. report fixed values for current density and Faradaic efficiency, we allow them to vary within realistic engineering ranges to reflect performance variability during scale-up. We incorporate the most impactful parameters as sources of uncertainty into a simulation-based optimization framework proposed by Al et al. (2020). This framework enables efficient evaluation of robust reactor designs and operating strategies that balance process efficiency, utility demand, and economic performance under uncertain conditions. Preliminary results suggest that continuous operation can deliver promising conversion and energy efficiency under moderate current densities. The case study reveals trade-offs between electrochemical performance and overall cost, reinforcing the value of early-stage modeling for practical design decisions. In future work, we will conduct a comparative analysis between this continuous electrochemical process and the chemical multi-step ibuprofen synthesis route. This comparison will focus on energy use, sustainability metrics, and overall process economics. Our findings aim to support the broader transition toward electrified, modular, and sustainable pharmaceutical production systems. References Mena, S., Sanchez, J., & Guirado, G. (2019). https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Mechanistic Modeling of the Formation of Incomplete and Mispaired Multispecific Antibodies
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Multispecific antibodies are a novel class of therapeutic drug molecules that can simultaneously bind multiple targets. Unlike that of traditional monospecific antibodies, the immunoglobulin chains forming the structure of a multispecific antibody are heterogeneous. As such, correct intracellular assembly is critical to the formation of the desired target molecule. Despite protein engineering efforts to favor the correct configuration, incomplete fragments and mispaired species are still commonly observed in the manufacturing of multispecifics, leading to higher levels of low molecular weight (LMW) impurities that are difficult to clear. To address this challenge, we present a practical mechanistic model that captures the process of mispaired species and LMW formation. After calibration with experimental data, the model can be used for in silico optimizations, nominating conditions that minimize the unwanted impurities. Overall, our work illustrates an example of how mechanistic modeling can accelerate upstream development in new drug modality settings.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Degradation in PEO- B -PCL Films and the Role of Crystalline Morphology
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: PEO- b -PCL (polyethylene oxide- b -polycaprolactone) is an amphiphilic block copolymer that has gained a lot of attention for its biomedical applications. These copolymers are somewhat unique in that the T m s of each block are similar. While crystal formation drives phase separation, the crystal development and relative crystallinities impacts their macroscopic properties. Our previous work has shown that film crystallization behavior can be manipulated using typical techniques such as selective solvent casting and thermal history. Interestingly, when using particular selective solvents, the crystal morphology switches from edge-on spherulites to flat-on lamellae. Because these polymers are valued for their degradation and drug release potential, we are investigating these properties as a function of each block's crystallinity and the overall crystal morphology. Here, the erosion and hydrolytic degradation of PEO- b -PCL films in aqueous solution were shown to vary with weight fraction, crystalline content, and morphology indicating the role of both PEO and PCL crystallization on water uptake, dissolution, and chain decomposition. Additionally, environmental factors such as pH and temperature of the aqueous solution were evaluated.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Protein Language-Based Model for Cell-Penetrating Biopolymers in Multi- Cargo Intracellular Delivery
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Biopolymers are promising candidates for therapeutic applications in diseases such as cancer and neurodegenerative disorders. Among them, cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) facilitate the intracellular delivery of therapeutic and diagnostic cargo, including small molecules, proteins, and oligonucleotides. While machine learning (ML) approaches have proven effective in predicting CPPs using sequence-based features, existing methods often rely on a limited set of handcrafted descriptors. Recent advances in transformers and large language models (LLMs) suggest that self-supervised learning can extract more informative sequence features, surpassing traditional feature engineering in predictive performance. Our study develops a protein language model-based approach to design and analyze CPPs for delivering small peptides (5–10 amino acids) as cargo inside cells. We leverage pretrained protein language models (ESM variants, BEPLER, and ProtBERT) to generate sequence embeddings, which are fed into a deep learning model using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for binary classification of CPPs. Unlike conventional approaches, our model considers CPP sequences with and without cargo as distinct inputs, enabling predictions of whether a given CPP remains functional after cargo loading. To complement our ML-based predictions, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations are used to investigate CPP-membrane interactions, providing deeper insights into their biophysical properties. In summary, our study integrates machine learning and MD simulations to advance the understanding and design of CPPs, with potential applications in drug delivery, gene therapy, and precision medicine, where efficient intracellular transport of biomolecules remains a significant challenge.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: AI-Driven End-to-End Digital Twins for Pharmaceutical Process Development
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Digital twins are increasingly recognised as valuable tools in pharmaceutical process development, offering virtual models that support design, control, and optimisation. However, their adoption remains challenging, not only due to the technical complexity but also because developing comprehensive end-to-end process models has traditionally required expertise spanning multiple disciplines. Historically, a team of specialists was necessary to navigate process interdependencies and extract meaningful insights. In this presentation, we explore how AI-driven workflows can help bridge these gaps, empowering individuals to construct and interpret end-to-end digital twins with greater confidence. By guiding users past common blockers—such as selecting an appropriate modelling approach when data is sparse—our framework facilitates the integration of mechanistic, hybrid, and data-driven models. We illustrate this through case studies demonstrating how AI-driven agents suggest structured modelling workflows grounded in process systems engineering principles. These workflows serve as stepwise guides, enabling scientists to progress systematically from experimentation to model-based insights. Beyond the technical aspects, we discuss the regulatory and practical challenges that must be addressed to integrate these digital twins into pharmaceutical development. By lowering the barriers to process modelling, we aim to provide a framework that enhances accessibility, enabling broader adoption of AI-driven digital twins and ultimately supporting more efficient, insight-driven drug development.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Dissecting Cr-Doped Interfaces: How Diffusion Dynamics Reshape the Van Der Waals Gap and Shift Sb₂Te₃ Thermoelectric Performance
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: The development of advanced thermoelectric materials is crucial for sustainable energy conversion and efficient waste heat recovery. Among promising candidates, Sb₂Te₃ is recognized for its exceptional thermoelectric performance near room temperature and its classification as a topological insulator, offering potential for spintronic and quantum computing applications. However, the structural and electronic effects induced by doping, particularly transition metals such as chromium (Cr), are not fully understood, especially concerning the critical role of the intrinsic van der Waals (vdW) gap. In this study, we employ an integrated approach combining density functional theory (DFT), ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD), nudged elastic band (NEB) calculations, machine learning (ML) techniques, and experimental validations to systematically investigate how Cr doping influences the structural, electronic, and thermoelectric properties of Sb₂Te₃. Benchmarking studies confirm the necessity of incorporating van der Waals corrections and spin-orbit coupling (SOC) for accurately modeling these systems, which possess significant relativistic and layered interactions. We find that Cr atoms preferentially occupy substitutional sites rather than interstitial positions within the lattice, significantly altering the thermodynamic stability and the vdW gap. Detailed analysis of Cr migration pathways reveals that diffusion mechanisms and migration barriers are critically dependent on the vdW gap dimensions, creating a complex interplay that dictates the final doping configuration and stability. Our results indicate that vdW gap modulation induced by Cr doping leads to substantial structural changes and significant shifts in electronic band structure, notably influencing the positions of Dirac points at the Γ and A points. Manual adjustments of the vdW gap distance in pristine Sb₂Te₃, independent of Cr doping, further underscore the direct relationship between vdW gap alterations and electronic bandstructure transformations. To disentangle the mechanical and magnetic effects of Cr, we conducted additional simulations removing Cr atoms post-relaxation. These simulations confirm that structural modifications in the vdW gap alone substantially affect electronic behavior, highlighting the vdW gap as a central descriptor influencing electronic properties. AIMD simulations conducted at room temperature reveal dynamic evolution of vdW gaps, emphasizing their stability and sensitivity to realistic operating conditions. Additionally, simulations under external pressure demonstrate the mechanical robustness of the Cr-doped system and provide insights into alternative strategies for vdW gap tuning beyond chemical doping. Using BoltzTraP2 calculations, we quantify the impact of Cr doping on thermal transport properties, revealing that variations in vdW gap distances significantly enhance phonon scattering, particularly in the low-frequency regime. This leads to reductions in lattice thermal conductivity and improvements in thermoelectric performance. Consequently, we propose that the vdW gap dimension can serve as a potent, tunable parameter to optimize thermoelectric materials. Ultimately, this comprehensive study provides a novel framework integrating computational modeling, machine learning-driven design, and experimental validation, establishing a closed-loop, autonomous approach for materials discovery. Our findings position the vdW gap as a critical, predictive descriptor within machine learning models, facilitating the targeted design of multifunctional thermoelectric and spintronic materials.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Experimental and Theoretical Studies of an Aminosilane As Inhibitor to Achieve Area-Selective Deposition of HfO 2 on SiO 2
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: The ongoing miniaturization of semiconductor devices drives the development of efficient and robust device manufacturing techniques. Current device fabrication integrates a wide range of nanomaterials via time-consuming, top-down patterning approaches involving hundreds of deposition, lithography, etch, and stripping steps. Area selective deposition is a promising bottom-up technique that directly deposits a patterned layer through surface treatment. Amongst vapor phase deposition techniques, atomic layer deposition (ALD) harnesses self-limiting surface chemistries to deposit uniform, pinhole-free, conformal thin films over high-aspect ratio structures. Area-selective atomic layer deposition engages the advantages of both to achieve selective deposition with precise control over film thickness and properties. Typically, inhibitors such as self-assembled monolayers and small molecule inhibitors are used to facilitate selective growth on one surface over another. However, their carbonaceous groups may lead to undesired carbon contamination and thereby compromised device performance. This study uses experimental and computational methods to explore bisdiethylaminosilane (BDEAS) as an inhibitor against HfO 2 ALD on a native SiO 2 surface. BDEAS forms a carbon-free –SiH 2 terminated inhibition layer via bidentate chemisorption to surface hydroxyl groups, which otherwise would serve as ALD active sites. Density functional theory (DFT) modeling demonstrates inherent selectivity of BDEAS adsorption on hydroxyl- rather than amine-terminated surfaces. Key process parameters are identified from first principles, and corresponding process controls — vapor pressure, dosing time, and soaking time — are tuned to identify the optimal inhibitor deposition regime. The blocking ability of BDEAS is quantified experimentally and compared with that of di-isopropylaminosilane (DIPAS), an inhibitor which forms –SiH 3 terminations. Compared to DIPAS, the blocking ability of BDEAS is limited because of less favorable polydentate chemisorption energetics and steric hinderance from its dual reactive groups. Experimental results indicate that BDEAS has less blocking ability than DIPAS due to the degradation of the inhibition layer with hafnium precursor pulses. Theoretical calculations of energetics along the reaction coordinate reveal key differences in reaction mechanisms and resulting surface terminations of the two inhibitors, shedding light on their respective inhibitor layer degradation mechanisms. Post-deposition annealing targeted at improving resistance of the inhibition layer to precursor-induced degradation improves BDEAS blocking ability as confirmed experimentally. DFT modeling show changes in reaction energetics arising from the anneal which explain the blocking ability differences. Overall, this study demonstrates the impact of denticity and ligand size in determining inhibitor blocking ability and showcases how effective choices of inhibitor molecule, post-deposition processing, and ALD process work synergistically to achieve selectivity and enable bottom-up integration of nanomaterials for device fabrication.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Optimizing La/Sr Ratio in La y Sr 1-Y Ni 0.5 Mg 0.5 O 3 Perovskites for Enhanced Catalytic Performance in Dry Reforming of Methane
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Enhancing catalyst stability and efficiency in dry reforming of methane (DRM) is essential for syngas production, requiring materials with high activity and resistance to carbon deposition. This study explores the impact of Sr substitution for La in La y Sr 1-y Ni 0.5 Mg 0.5 O 3 perovskites, emphasizing their structural integrity, oxygen mobility, and catalytic properties. XRD analysis confirms the formation of well-crystallized perovskites, while TPR and XPS reveal that Sr incorporation increases oxygen vacancies, stabilizing the lattice and shifting Ni reduction to higher temperatures. The La-rich composition (y = 1) demonstrates the highest catalytic activity, reaching 88% CO 2 and 75% CH 4 conversion at 750 °C. Conversely, the Sr-rich sample (y = 0) shows enhanced oxygen vacancy formation and basicity but lower catalytic efficiency, with 27% CO 2 and 20% CH 4 conversion at 500 °C, due to SrCO 3 formation reducing active site availability. The interaction between La and Sr plays a crucial role in tuning Ni reducibility, where La promotes Ni reduction, while Sr delays low-temperature reduction. La 0.5 Sr 0.5 Ni 0.5 Mg 0.5 O 3 achieves an optimal balance of oxygen mobility and catalytic performance, effectively minimizing coke formation. The incorporation of Mg further enhances stability and CO 2 adsorption. However, excessive La content increases carbon deposition, emphasizing the need for a carefully adjusted La/Sr ratio. These findings highlight the significance of La/Sr composition in optimizing perovskite catalysts for DRM, providing valuable insights into their structural and catalytic properties for efficient syngas production. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Thermal Conversion of Cotton Gin Byproducts into Liquid Fuels and High-Value Chemicals
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Cotton Gin Byproducts (CGB) have become a major challenge for the cotton ginning industry over the years due to the large volume of material produced annually, leading to issues associated with their handling and proper disposal. CGB are composed mainly of cotton burrs, motes, sticks, leaf parts, and fine woody particles, which are generated by various equipment in the ginning process, mainly during seed cotton and lint cleaning. Studies on CGB suggest that they have significant potential as a biofuel feedstock due to their cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin composition, like other widely studied agricultural residues such as rice straw, wheat straw, etc. Thermochemical methods of conversion have emerged as promising approaches to convert biomass into liquid fuels for (bio)energy applications, including upgrades for use as transportation fuel. However, the potential of these thermochemical processes for efficiently converting CGB into biofuels remains largely unexplored. In this study, we investigate the potential of converting CGB into liquid fuel and high-value chemicals through three thermochemical processes: fast pyrolysis, catalytic pyrolysis, and hydropyrolysis. Five CGB samples were collected from equipment at different stages of the ginning process (cylinder cleaners, stick machine, and the “trash master”) at the USDA-ARS micro-gin in Stoneville, MS. Preliminary proximate analysis revealed an average volatile matter of 69 wt.%, 7.3 wt.% fixed carbon, 10 wt.% moisture content, and ash content of 10 wt.% across the five CGB samples. The average carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, sulfur, and oxygen contents were found to be 43.5%, 4.7%, 2.8%, 0.4%, and 37.5 wt.%, respectively. The higher heating value ranged from 15 to 17 MJ/kg. In this work, we initially subject the CGB samples to fast pyrolysis in a CDS Analytical Pyroprobe at a temperature of 500°C, and the resulting pyrolysis vapors are analyzed using Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry/Flame Ionization Detector (GC-MS/FID) to determine their chemical composition and product distribution. We also investigate the effect of catalytic pyrolysis using conventional HZSM-5 and a modified zeolite catalyst (2D-nanosheets) to enhance the selectivity to aromatic compounds while minimizing undesired oxygenated compounds. The samples will also be converted in the presence of hydrogen (hydropyrolysis) to assess the effect of hydrogenation of the pyrolysis products into aromatics and cycloalkanes. Previous studies have demonstrated that hydropyrolysis and the use of metal-doped zeolites improve the degree of deoxygenation and promote the formation of aromatics such as benzene, toluene, and xylenes (BTX), which are critical intermediates for fuel applications. We hypothesize that the variability in the composition of the CGB from the different stages in the ginning process will result in distinct product distributions, and that modified 2D nanosheet zeolites will outperform conventional HZSM-5 catalysts in increasing the yield of aromatic hydrocarbons. Furthermore, we expect hydropyrolysis to produce higher hydrocarbon yields by reducing oxygenates through hydrodeoxygenation. We are confident our findings will contribute to the development of improved thermochemical processes for converting cotton gin byproducts into liquid fuels and high-value chemicals, which can serve to reduce the abundance of this agricultural byproduct, provide transportation liquid fuels, and ultimately advance sustainable fuel production.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Assessing the Impact of Biomass Burning on Air Quality in West Bengal
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Biomass burning is widely believed to be a contributor to poor air quality in Indo Gangetic Plain (IGP) region in India, but its contribution within the state of West Bengal is not well recognized. This is partly due to the dominance of other pollution sources in the region and differences in harvest schedules compared to other parts of the IGP. This study integrates remote sensing data along with ground-level PM2.5 measurements in an attempt to establish a data-driven association between biomass burning and air quality across multiple districts in West Bengal. Remote sensing data is used to capture fire activity across the state along with data on trace gases concentrations. A network of over 220 low-cost sensors is used to obtain ground based PM2.5 measurements across the state at high spatio-temporal resolution. By aligning weekly fire activity with district-level PM2.5 data, we perform a spatiotemporal analysis to quantify the impact of biomass burning on PM2.5 concentration across the state. The concentrations of co-emitted trace gases such as CO, NO₂, SO 2 , NH 4 derived from remote sensing data is also incorporated into the analysis to isolate biomass burning from other contributors. Correlation analyses are conducted to evaluate the statistical association between fire activity and PM2.5 concentrations. Preliminary results show a strong correlation between fire incidents and localized PM2.5 surges, particularly during peak burning periods in some districts. While this observation holds true for certain agricultural areas, other districts show a relatively weaker association, suggesting that crop burning may play a lesser role in those regions. The effect of cross-state transport and regional contribution is also studies in this work. These findings provide a more quantitative understanding of biomass burning’s role in overall air quality across the state of West Bengal.

The morphology and autosense efficiency of modified PNAs are drastically different and seemingly strongly correlated. We will demonstrate SAXS can be a powerful tool to identify nanoscale morphology and determine the aggregation behavior.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Trust Region Bayesian Optimization with Tanimoto Similarity for Efficient, Scalable, and Progressive Molecular Design
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Molecular property optimization (MPO) – the task of identifying molecules with desirable physicochemical or functional properties – is central to fields such as drug discovery, materials design, and catalysis [1]. MPO problems are notoriously difficult: molecular spaces are discrete, structured, and high-dimensional, and property evaluations (e.g., quantum mechanical calculations or experimental synthesis) are typically expensive. Traditional optimization methods struggle in these settings due to limited sample efficiency and an inability to handle complex chemical structure-property relationships [2]. Bayesian optimization (BO) [3] provides a promising framework for such problems, as it is explicitly designed to be sample-efficient in black-box settings. However, standard BO methods often assume continuous design spaces and can fail when applied to molecular domains. They may propose structurally unrealistic candidates, make large and experimentally infeasible jumps across chemical space, or depend on representations that do not respect chemical validity. These limitations are particularly problematic in experimental settings, where chemists favor incremental, synthetically tractable changes to known compounds. Moreover, while data-driven molecular generators such as variational autoencoders (VAEs) [4, 5, 6] can provide a workaround by learning continuous latent spaces, they require large training datasets and can produce invalid or unrealistic molecules, limiting their utility in early-stage discovery or low-data regimes. To address these limitations, we introduce TuRBO-Mol, a novel trust-region Bayesian optimization algorithm tailored for practical, progressive molecular design. TuRBO-Mol extends the original TuRBO algorithm [7] (originally developed for high-dimensional continuous spaces) to discrete molecular spaces by constructing dynamic trust regions based on Tanimoto similarity between molecular fingerprints. These trust regions adaptively expand when the model discovers better-performing molecules and contract otherwise, enabling localized, sample-efficient exploration that reflects synthetic accessibility. Rather than relying on pre-defined libraries or latent space models, TuRBO-Mol generates candidate molecules on-the-fly via realistic structural perturbations such as atom or functional group substitutions. This search strategy mirrors how chemists reason about chemical modifications, ensuring that candidates remain both valid and synthetically relevant throughout the optimization process. We evaluate TuRBO-Mol on multiple benchmark MPO tasks, demonstrating that it achieves competitive or superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods while requiring significantly fewer evaluations. Notably, we present what we believe is the first application of trust-region BO to the computational discovery of non-precious metal catalysts for the oxygen reduction reaction using density functional theory simulations. Across tasks, TuRBO-Mol consistently produces diverse, high-quality molecules and scales effectively to large, unstructured chemical spaces. These results position TuRBO-Mol as a practical and interpretable approach for molecular design, bridging the gap between theoretical BO and the constraints of real-world chemistry workflows. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Assessing Shortcut Behavior in Tulip Vessels with Lattice Boltzmann Method and Reduced Order Models
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Diafiltration and ultrafiltration (UF/DF) are critical processing steps for the production of biomolecules such as proteins. They are often used in tandem: while ultrafiltration increases the concentration of the target product in the solution, diafiltration exchanges the buffer to remove solvents and salts from the solution. Tulip vessels are a popular choice for UF/DF processes because they allow low minimal working volumes for high product concentrations. However, the tulip design has the potential of short-circuiting. Due to this shortcut, a part of the higher product concentration from the retentate flow reaches the feed flow before it is completely mixed in the vessel. The results are unexpectedly high product concentrations, higher viscosity of the solution, poor filter performance and in extreme cases, filter clogging. The shortcut rate depends on operating conditions, such as mixing speed and recirculation flow rate, and material properties. Thus, each process and operating conditions have a characteristic shortcut rate. In this work, we focus on the diafiltration step. Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) has become the tool of choice for the numerical study of mixing processes inside stirred tanks [1]. In the presented work, we have used an in-house CFD code based on Lattice Boltzmann method (LBM). Beside the fluid flow calculation, a passive scalar equation has been implemented to track the protein concentrations. In the presented work, we have defined the shortcut rate as a difference between the concentration at tank outlet surface and volume averaged concentration inside the tank. Larger concentration at outlet surface as inside the tank, identified the shortcut. In the simulation, the shortcut is calculated using a tracer and passive scalar respectively. At the beginning, the tracer concentration in the tank volume is set to zero and at the outlet equal to one. The difference between these two concentrations is monitored. This difference peaks at the start of the process and reduces over time to zero when perfect mixing is achieved. The diafiltration process itself requires long process times in the order of hours. Thus, the results of the LBM simulations are used to parametrize a reduced order model. The reduced order model is a reactor network model with a feedback loop: The concentration at the vessel inlet (filter retentate flow) depends on the concentration at the vessel outlet (filter feed flow). The reduced order model predicts the time to exchange the buffer, and the expected increase in product concentration at the outlet surface during diafiltration. The LBM simulations yielded shortcut rates in the range of 10%-30% for a given set of operating conditions. Choosing process conditions with a higher throughput at the cost of increased shortcut behavior can be a valid process design decision to reduce the process time. The reduced order model quantifies the increase in product concentration and the relative increase in process time due to the shortcut, allowing for better process design decisions.
