https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Metal–Phenolic Scaffolds for Enhanced Electron Transfer in Enzymatic Systems
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Electrocatalysis, especially in cascade enzymatic systems, is often hindered by inefficient electron transfer between sequential enzymes. To overcome this challenge, we developed a strategy that integrates metal–phenolic networks (MPNs) with enzymatic catalysis. This was achieved by combining naturally occurring polyphenols—tannic acid, gallic acid, and lignin—with transition metal ions like copper, cobalt, and iron, forming functional coatings on electrode surfaces. Using electropolymerization on screen-printed electrodes, we established stable MPN layers capable of encapsulating and supporting electrochemical enzymatic reactions. Glucose oxidase and horseradish peroxidase were employed as model enzymes for their complementary redox properties, forming an interconnected catalytic cycle. We systematically evaluated the performance of these enzyme cascades across various MPN compositions to identify the most effective combinations for enhancing bioelectrocatalytic activity. This platform offers a promising approach to improving electron transfer efficiency in biosensing and biofuel cell technologies.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Advancements in Electrocatalysis for Sustainable Hydrogen Production and CO2 Reduction
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: The quest for sustainable energy solutions has spurred significant advancements in electrochemical processes for hydrogen production and carbon dioxide reduction. We explored value-added electrolysis for green hydrogen production, emphasizing the importance of innovative materials in enhancing electrolysis efficiency. Further strengthening the catalytic landscape, we focused on electrocatalysts for coupled hydrogen evolution and demonstrated the sustainable synthesis of single-atom catalysts for iodide oxidation and partial oxidation reactions of ethylene glycol. In parallel efforts, we also showed a cooperative dual single-atom Ni/Cu catalyst, achieving the highly selective reduction of CO 2 to ethanol and addressing energy and environmental concerns. Additionally, we reported on electrochemical CO 2 reduction using catalytically harmonious Ni/Cu dual active sites to generate multi-carbon products, showcasing the versatility of dual catalysts in carbon utilization. These studies underscore the pivotal role of advanced electrocatalysis in driving sustainable energy technologies forward, emphasizing the integration of innovative materials and catalytic designs to achieve enhanced performance in electrochemical conversion processes.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Capacitively-Mediated Electrochemical Flow Reactors Enable Current Draw Beyond Mass Transfer Limits
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Mitigation of climate change demands parallel efforts in electrifying all industrial sectors, among which chemicals production and cost-effective grid-scale energy storage remain monumental standing challenges. In both spaces, electrification of heterogeneous reactions are prohibitively challenging due to solid-phase accumulation in traditional porous electrodes and due to solid-phase mass transfer being 3-5 orders of magnitude slower than liquid-phase mass transfer. Slurry electrodes solve both problems: flowable suspensions of electronically conductive particles enable continuous electrodeposition and double layer charging. The suspended particles can subsequently be advected away with the deposited solid phases – and similarly advect capacitively adsorbed charge. Controlling the residence time of the electrode allows modulation between orthogonal current sources: either primarily capacitive or faradaic current draw. In the capacitive regime, current draw from the double layer is unimpeded by faradaic mass transfer limits. As the capacitively charged electrode flows out of the cell, its stored surface charge drives reactions during equilibration—decoupling charge loading and reaction timescales. Here, we establish dimensionless operational and design criteria required to exploit this separation of reactive and capacitive timescales to allow continuous current draw beyond reactive rate limits. We leverage a 1D transient electrochemical model to resolve capacitive, faradaic, and mass transport timescales, providing critical insight into power-density implications of each operating regime on cell-level performance for energy storage applications, but also the extent to which a reaction can be driven outside the electrochemical reactor. Ultimately, we propose design strategies that bypass reactive rate limitations by "electrochemical-looping", whereby charge is loaded onto the double layer in the electrochemical cell and a faradaic reaction is driven by the discharge of the double layer outside the cell. This separation of charge loading unlocks high-rate operation of electrochemical reactors utilizing sluggish chemistries -- overcoming rate limitations in critical sectors such as chemical synthesis and grid-scale storage.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Scaling up the Height of CO 2 Electrolysers Using a Falling Film Catholyte
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Meeting global energy transition goals requires significant reductions in CO 2 emissions. Low-temperature CO 2 electrolysis represents a promising strategy, enabling both the mitigation of onsite CO 2 emissions and the production of valuable chemicals. While substantial progress has been made in improving the efficiency of CO 2 reduction – particularly through the use of gas diffusion electrodes (GDEs) in flow cells with liquid catholyte – most studies remain limited to small, lab-scale systems. A major challenge now lies in scaling these electrolysers to industrially relevant sizes. Although GDEs enable high current densities, scaling up the active area and especially the vertical height of electrolysers introduces several complications, including GDE flooding and uneven electrolyte distribution. These limitations demand innovative design strategies to facilitate industrial-scale CO 2 electrolysis. This study proposes a novel flow cell design combining a bipolar membrane operating under reverse bias with a gravity-driven falling film catholyte compartment (Fig. attached). The falling film approach offers minimal pressure drop even for reactors taller than 1 meter, while the bipolar membrane ensures the necessary ionic environment at the cathode, even at low catholyte flow rates. The investigation comprises two main parts: (i) fluid dynamics analysis using a standalone 1 m falling film setup to determine optimal geometry, and (ii) electrochemical testing in a 100 cm 2 CO 2 electrolyser.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Design Criteria for Direct Seawater Electrolysis Integrated with in-Situ Water Purification
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: To harness offshore renewable energy and saline water for green hydrogen production, direct seawater electrolysis has emerged as a promising approach. However, the presence of ions such as Cl⁻, Ca²⁺, and Mg²⁺ in seawater leads to electrode degradation and reduces Faradaic efficiency due to competing chloride oxidation, posing safety concerns. Conventional electrolysis systems use energy-intensive pretreatment steps, including reverse osmosis and ion exchange, to remove these impurities. To eliminate these processes, this project explores integrating in-situ water purification into electrolyzer using selective membranes—specifically forward osmosis (FO) and PTFE membranes. These membranes leverage osmotic or vapor pressure gradients to transport water into the electrolyzer while excluding unwanted ions, thus simplifying system design and energy demands. We developed a zero-gap water electrolyzer flow cell incorporating these membranes and quantified water transport rates via weight-change measurements to determine current density limits for steady-state operation. The selectivity of these membranes was evaluated using ion chromatography. Long-term performance and degradation were assessed over 40 hours through electrochemical and materials analysis. Results show that electrolyzers with FO membranes experienced pH imbalances between anolyte and catholyte due to sodium ion dominance, which suppressed proton migration. This caused acidity buildup, leading to anode corrosion and catalyst redeposition on the cathode. These effects highlight a critical limitation of the systems using FO membranes in near-neutral pH conditions. In contrast, systems using PTFE membranes demonstrated stable performance over 40 hours, with no significant degradation observed. Our findings identify key design parameters and limitations for scaling up in-situ purification strategies in seawater electrolysis, offering a pathway toward stable offshore hydrogen production without the need for traditional water pretreatment.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Strategies for Enhancing Activity, Selectivity, and Stability for Water Oxidation at Electrochemical Interfaces
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: The electrochemical oxidation of water is a key reaction in renewable energy technologies , resulting in the production of either oxygen gas (O 2 ) via the four -electron oxygen evolution reaction ( OER ) or hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ) through the two -electron water oxidation reaction ( 2e-WOR ) . While OER is the dominant pathway, it is kinetically hindered . On the other hand, the valuable H 2 O 2 production via 2e-WOR is often limited by poor selectivity. In my research, I employ various computational strategies to optimize the activity , selectivity , and stability of water oxidation reactions by performing density functional theory (DFT)-based thermodynamic and kinetic analys e s of the reaction pathways at electrochemical interfaces. I investigate active site properties on g raphene-based single- and dual-atom PGM-free catalysts , as well as explicit electrode/electrolyte interactions on IrO 2 , RuO 2 , and bicarbonate-adsorbed BiVO 4 electrocatalyst systems.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Mechanistic Insights into Electrochemical C–N Coupling for Sustainable Organonitrogen Synthesis
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Electrochemical synthesis of organonitrogen compounds from abundant C and N sources offers a sustainable route to valuable chemicals such as urea and cyclohexanone oxime. By leveraging CO 2 and NO 3 ⁻ species (or cyclohexanone and NO 2 ⁻) as feedstocks, this approach capitalizes on ambient-condition reactions that reduce reliance on fossil-based processes. Experimental trends indicate that product distributions shift significantly with pH and applied potential, reflecting the delicate balance between C–N coupling and competitive protonation pathways. To elucidate these complex reaction networks, we employ a suite of computational techniques including ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) with explicit solvation, constant potential DFT modeling with hybrid solvation, nudged elastic band (NEB) calculations, and enhanced sampling methods. These simulations identify key coupling pathways, *CO-*NOH, *CO-*NO, and *CO-*NO 2 , and reveal that moderate potentials favor the formation of these coupling products, whereas highly negative biases promote undesired protonation steps. Our integrated modeling framework pinpoints the rate-determining steps and energetic barriers that govern the electrochemical C–N bond formation across different systems. For instance, in the CO₂/NOₓ⁻ system, the formation of a *CO–NO 2 adduct is crucial, while in the cyclohexanone/NO 2 ⁻ pathway, controlled nitrite reduction enables selective oxime synthesis. The findings illustrate that both pH and electrode potential play pivotal roles in steering the reaction pathways, providing a molecular-level rationale for experimental observations. Ultimately, these insights offer a valuable foundation for the rational design of electrocatalysts that can precisely balance intermediate stabilization and reaction kinetics, thereby advancing the sustainable synthesis of a broad spectrum of C–N bond-containing products.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Radioactive Particle Tracking (RPT) Based Hydrodynamics Investigation in Slurry Phase Reactor for Residue Hydrocracking
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Slurry-phase hydrocracking pose a cutting-edge technology for transforming residual crude oil into low-sulfur diesel and gasoline, harnessing the dual objectives of meeting sustainable energy demand and complying with stringent environmental regulations. The efficiency and scalability of slurry phase reactors rely on a robust understanding of their hydrodynamics and reaction kinetics. Despite its industrial significance, detailed experimental data on key hydrodynamic parameters such as gas holdup, liquid velocity, solid dispersion, and turbulence in slurry-phase reactors remains sparse. This knowledge gap hinders precise reactor design and optimization. This study addresses these gaps by investigating local hydrodynamics using a non-invasive technique, radioactive particle tracking (RPT), under cold-flow conditions that replicate the physical properties of residue and hydrogen at hydrocracking reaction conditions. Experiments in a 0.1 m diameter, 1.2 m high bubble column leveraged a water-ethanol mixture to replicate the density and viscosity of residue and hydrogen under hydrocracking conditions of 425 °C and 160 bar. Co-60 radioactive particle technology was utilized to perform a comprehensive analysis of liquid hydrodynamics across both homogeneous and heterogeneous flow regimes. This approach enabled precise measurements of flow behavior, mixing efficiency, and transition dynamics. The findings from this work highlights the crucial insights into the hydrodynamics of slurry-phase reactors, paving the way for enhanced reactor design and scale-up strategies in industrial hydrocracking applications. Keywords: slurry-phase reactor, hydrocracking, hydrodynamics, Co-60, RPT

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Synthesis and Evaluation of TiO 2 /CdS Nanocomposite for Photocatalytic Degradation of Acetaminophen under Sunlight Activation
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Due to its photo stability, abundance, low cost, and strong oxidative potential, titanium dioxide (TiO 2 ) has been most widely studied semiconductor photocatalyst and therefore, has been popularly used for various applications, especially for degradation of organic contaminants from water. However, due to its limited activation to visible light, the modification strategies have been sought to enhance photocatalytic efficiency in visible light region. In this contribution, TiO 2 /CdS nanocomposites were synthesized in two molar ratios, 1:1 and 1:0.5 through a controlled chemical precipitation method to investigate their photocatalytic performance in the degradation of acetaminophen, an emerging water and wastewater pollutant and a common antipyretic and analgesic pharmaceutical. X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) techniques were used to validate the crystal structures, chemical bonding, and surface morphology of TiO 2 /CdS nanocomposites for visible light absorption. Photocatalytic degradation experiments were conducted under three experimental conditions using ambient natural sunlight irradiation for 7 hours in sunny day in May of 2024: (i) control sample under sunlight without catalyst, (ii) pure TiO 2 under sunlight, and (iii) 1:1 TiO 2 /CdS nanocomposite under sunlight. In the absence of a catalyst, little degradation of 7.58% was observed. Pure TiO 2 demonstrated only a little increase photocatalytic activity of 12.05% degradation under visible sunlight, attributed to its wide bandgap and rapid electron-hole recombination. Notably, the 1:1 TiO 2 /CdS nanocomposite achieved an enhanced degradation of 27.32% within the 7 hours of experiments conducted between 11 am to 6 pm. This enhancement in the degradation can be ascribed to the formation of a heterojunction between TiO 2 and CdS, which facilitated an improved visible light absorption and a better charge separation. The finding shows TiO 2 /CdS nanocomposite as a potential system for efficient and effective sunlight-driven photocatalysts for the advanced oxidative degradation of water/wastewater pharmaceutical contaminants.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Optimization of Catalytic Reactor Design for Carbon Efficient Ethylene Production from Natural Gas
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Ethylene is one of the largest volume chemicals and holds its significance in the petrochemical industry to produce variety of chemical intermediates and polymers. Yet, production of ethylene is almost exclusively limited to highly energy intensive ethane steam cracking. Researchers have extensively studied oxidative dehydrogenation of ethane (ODHE) and oxidative coupling of methane (OCM) to produce ethylene with lower energy consumption. However, both the processes are limited to commercialization due to heat management concerns. In this work, we demonstrate the feasibility of carrying out these partial oxidation reactions in an autothermal monolith reactor through comprehensive bifurcation analysis. We use a multi-scale reduced order model that accounts for pore diffusion to analyze the ignition-extinction behavior during ODHE in a monolith reactor coated with a MoVTeNbO x (M1) catalyst. Our modeling results indicate that metallic monoliths with intermediate length, high substrate conductivity and high cell density are optimal to approach the so called “homogeneous lumped thermal reactor (LTR) limit” which leads to the best reactor performance (92% ethylene selectivity at 25% ethane conversion). It is also shown that operation of the reactor in the external mass or heat transfer controlled regime with strong interphase gradients can lower ethylene selectivity. We compare OCM (La 2 O 3 /CaO-catalyst) and ODHE (M1-catalyst) from a kinetic perspective, highlighting the impact of species back-mixing and operating temperature on ethylene formation. The presence of oxygen gradient with uniform temperature improves ethylene selectivity in ODHE, whereas lower oxygen concentrations favor ethylene production in OCM. Moreover, ethylene yield can be further improved via cofeeding ethane with methane for which direct shale (natural) gas can be utilized. Our modelling results provide critical insights to design a CO 2 (thermal) free reactor with high throughput, thereby aiding the scale-up of ODHE and OCM to commercial level.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Going Beyond Oxygen Reduction Reaction: Nitrogen-Doped Carbon Nanostructures (CNx) As Catalysts for Electrocatalytic Hydrogenation of p-Nitrophenol in Acidic Medium
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Nitrogen-doped carbon nanostructures (CNx) have emerged as effective electrocatalysts for oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) in fuel cells. Ozkan group was first to demonstrate the ORR activity of CNx in acidic medium. Subsequently, these catalysts have also shown activity for halogen evolution and oxygen evolution reactions 1, 2 . In this study, we show that precious metal-free CNx is active for electrocatalytic hydrogenation (ECH) of p-nitrophenol in acidic medium. P-nitrophenol (p-NP) is a toxic contaminant found in wastewater from agrochemical industry and polluted groundwater. It has been classified as “priority pollutant” by US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) 3 . Treatment of p-NP in wastewater streams usually involves thermo-catalytic hydrogenation using strong reducing agents such as sodium borohydride (NaBH 4 ) or high-pressure hydrogen gas, in the presence of precious metal-based catalysts. ECH offers a safer alternative, as hydrogenation occurs via protons instead of high-pressure hydrogen or strong reducing agents. Most ECH studies involve expensive noble metal catalysts, necessitating the need of exploring cost-effective alternatives such as CNx. Our linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) tests demonstrated the electrocatalytic activity of CNx for reduction of p-NP with onset potential > 0 V vs reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE), hinting that p-NP ECH was more favorable than the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) (E o = 0 V vs RHE). In blank electrolyte (without p-NP), no significant current was observed indicating that competitive HER does not contribute appreciably to the observed hydrogenation current. Additionally, potential hold experiments confirmed the quantifiable reduction of p-NP using UV-Visible spectroscopic analysis. These preliminary results indicate promising activity of CNx for ECH of p-NP without using any precious metal or handling of high-pressure hydrogen gas/strong reducing agents. References: (1) Mamtani et al. Applied Catalysis B: Environmental 2018 , 220 , 88-97. (2) Jain et al. Journal of Catalysis 2022 , 413 , 1005-1016. (3) Serrà et al. Catalysts 2020 , 10 (4), 458.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Seeking Optimal Absorbent for in-Situ Conversion of CO 2 to Methanol: A Holistic Approach Combining Experiments, DFT Calculations, and Machine Learning.
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: In-situ conversion of CO₂ to methanol is an integrated approach combining CO₂ capture and catalytic conversion in a single step, thereby avoiding the energy-intensive regeneration of absorbents. This integration offers significant economic and environmental advantages, yet current in-situ conversion systems suffer from limited reaction performance compared to hydrogenation of pure CO₂ feedstocks. The key challenge is to identify an optimal CO₂ absorbent that performs effectively under in-situ conversion conditions to bridge this efficiency gap. In this study, we present a holistic approach combining machine learning (ML), density functional theory (DFT) calculations, and experimental evaluation. First, an ML model was developed to explore the space of potential CO₂ conversion pathways under in-situ conditions, providing mechanistic insights into intermediate formation and consumption. Next, DFT calculations were performed to determine the rate-determining step and to identify quantifiable molecular features of amine-based absorbents that correlate with high methanol yield. These features informed the construction of the second ML model for screening a broad library of candidate amines and predicting their performance. Top-ranked amines from this screening were subsequently validated in experiments, confirming improved CO₂-to-methanol conversion performance in line with the model predictions. This integrated study revealed a notable mechanistic insight: structurally hindered amines (with bulky substituents) do not readily form coordination complexes with the homogeneous catalyst, instead react with CO₂-derived formic acid to efficiently form amides (formamide intermediates). Even more surprisingly, we found that the presence of CO 2 can inhibit formation of amine-cat complexes, thereby enhancing methanol selectivity. This suggests that under in-situ conditions, CO 2 may act not merely as a reactant but as a reagent that governs the reaction selectivity. Our findings shed light on the selectivity mechanisms governing the formic acid–amide–methanol pathway in in-situ thermochemical CO₂-to-methanol conversion, offering a deeper understanding of the process that has not been elucidated in previous studies.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Elucidating the Effect of Charge Compensating Species on Aluminum-Oxygen Bond Cleavage in the Dissolution of the Faujasite Framework
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: In the synthesis of SSZ-39, The faujasite framework (FAU) is often used as both a silicon and an aluminum source. Due to the presence of double six membered rings in both SSZ-39 and FAU it has been suggested the double six membered rings (D6MRs) remain intact during synthesis and reconnect to form SSZ-39. If D6MRs remain intact this could lead to faster synthesis and would mean product aluminum distributions would be heavily influenced by parent aluminum distributions. In FAU there are 4 symmetrically distinct Al-O bonds (see Figure 1A), only one of which, the Al-O4 bond, can be broken without damaging the D6MR. This presents an opportunity to evaluate the feasibility of preserving D6MRs during synthesis since Al-O4 bonds should be more favorable to break than other Al-O bonds for D6MR subunits to remain intact. Using DFT calculations we compare the thermodynamic and kinetic favorability of cleaving Al-O4 bonds (see Figure 1B) compared to the favorability of cleaving other Al-O bonds to determine if the preservation of D6MRs in the interconversion of FAU to other zeolite frameworks is realistic. Reaction barriers were found to be sensitive to the Al-O bond being broken, with cleaving the Al-O4 bond having the highest reaction barrier of 1.63 eV and cleaving the Al-O2 bond having the lowest reaction barrier of 0.83 eV. These results suggest the D6MRs are not preserved during the interconversion of FAU to other zeolites since the Al-O4 bond is the only bond that can be cleaved without damaging the D6MR and it is the most difficult bond to cleave. Preliminary results with spectator species such as sodium atoms and organic structure directing agents show dealumination barriers are also sensitive to the chemical environment during dealumination, suggesting dealumination pathways can be controlled by modifying the chemical environment during zeolite interconversion.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Isopotential Electron Titration: The Mechanics of Quantifying Extent of Charge Transfer
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: A key challenge in heterogeneous catalysis is optimizing product selectivity while minimizing energy input. Charge transfer between an adsorbate and catalyst surface, which dictates binding energy and catalytic activity, can be used to identify desired reaction mechanisms. However, measuring charge transfer under reaction conditions is limited. Isopotential Electron Titration (IET) offers a rapid, non-destructive technique for quantifying metal-adsorbate charge transfer in-situ, making it an asset for advancing catalysis in academic and industrial settings. Extent of charge transfer was measured by switching bulk-phase hydrogen activity while forcing a metal-insulator-semiconductor (MIS) based catalyst to electrochemical equilibrium. This was accomplished by applying a potential drop of 0 V across the MIS stack, eliminating net current flow. Once equilibrium was reached, 100% hydrogen was introduced and adsorbed onto the surface, pulling the system out of equilibrium, and generating a measurable charge that titrated through an external circuit. When the new equilibrium state was achieved, 0.5% hydrogen was introduced to measure charge transfer from hydrogen desorption (Figure 1). Control experiments confirmed negligible hydrodynamic and thermal conductivity effects. Results showed that hydrogen adsorption induced a net charge transfer to the platinum surface, scaling linearly with temperature. Normalized per hydrogen atom, each donated 1.89 ± 0.005 mm e⁻ mol Pt⁻¹, consistent with a Bader charge analysis, which predicted 4 mm e⁻ mol Pt⁻¹. An equal and opposite charge transfer occurred upon desorption. This study presents an electronic approach to understanding catalyst surfaces and how metal-adsorbate charge transfer influences catalytic properties such as rate and selectivity. This methodology extends beyond hydrogen to key molecules like carbon monoxide, oxygen, and ammonia, supporting improved catalyst design and optimization strategies.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Comprehensive Thermodynamic Analysis and Reactor Modelling of CO 2 Conversion to Methanol
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: The potential benefit of converting CO 2 into methanol is twofold- mitigation of CO 2 and production of a valuable fuel having high octane number which can also be used for manufacturing other hydrocarbons and polymers. There are numerous studies on the conversion of syngas into methanol where the typical conversion with traditional catalyst (Cu/Zn) is limited to 25%. Consequently, there is no clear picture of the process and mechanism of conversion of pure CO 2 into methanol. First, the thermodynamic aspects of methanol synthesis for different operating conditions were investigated. The equilibrium conversion of CO 2 to methanol was determined for both isothermal and adiabatic cases from numerical solution of coupled chemical equilibrium relations and fugacity equations based on PR and SRK equation of state. Simulation results show that equilibrium constant and fugacity coefficient of CO 2 hydrogenation reaction were sensitive towards Gibbs free energy of formation and specific heat capacity of methanol. In the operating range of interest (400 – 600 K, 30 – 50 bar) CO 2 conversion varies from 40 % to 15 % suggesting that CO 2 hydrogenation is thermodynamically more favorable at low temperature and high pressure. Adiabatic temperature rise was observed to be 95 K for a feed composition of 1:5 (CO 2 :H 2 ) making it crucial to remove heat for obtaining higher yield of methanol. Next, the methanol synthesis reaction with Cu/Zn/Al 2 O 3 catalyst was investigated in CSTR and PFR configurations. The effect of different operating parameters such as feed composition, temperature and pressure on the conversion of CO 2 and yield of methanol was thoroughly analyzed. Our results imply that an optimum CO 2 conversion can be achieved while minimizing the effect of RWGS reaction at 450K -550K and 35 bar - 45 bar for a feed composition of 1:5. These results can be beneficial in developing potential technology applicable at industrial scale.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Unraveling Fluoride's Structure Directing Role on Zeolite Self-Assembly Via Integrated DFT and Monte Carlo Simulation
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Zeolites are nanoporous aluminosilicate materials with high specific surface area, regular pore sizes, strong acidity, and ion exchange capacity. Zeolites are widely applied in various fields, including catalysis, separations, and storage. There is increasing demand for zeolites, including tailor-made zeolite structures, to reach sustainability-related goals such as catalyzing biofuel production and capturing carbon dioxide. However, achieving precise control over the synthesis remains a significant challenge due to the complex interplay of factors within the sol-gel systems. As one of the key factors influencing zeolite formation, fluoride anion plays a significant structure-directing role in stabilizing key building blocks such as the double-4-membered ring (D4R). A thorough comprehension of the interactions between sol-gel silica and fluoride anions is dominant in unraveling the intricate zeolite self-assembly pathways. We integrate density functional theory (DFT) calculations with Reactive Ensemble Monte Carlo (RxMC) simulations, which successfully capture the zeolite formation kinetics and the complex interaction between the Si framework and the organic structure-directing template. A multi-step strategy is taken: (1) Recognizing the structural diversity of fluoride-silica interactions and the need for energetic accuracy, gas-phase electronic energy calculations via DFT generate a comprehensive energy dataset detailing the evolution of silica clusters. (2) The constructed energy dataset refines the acceptance probabilities within the RxMC simulations, enabling an accurate representation of the energetic landscape governing fluoride-mediated zeolite assembly. (3) To validate the computational predictions, the local fluoride environments within the developing framework are benchmarked with experimental data obtained through various spectroscopic techniques, including Nuclear Magnetic Resonance and Raman spectroscopy. By capturing the essential energetic driving forces at a fundamental level and incorporating them into a statistical simulation, our approach aims to bridge the gap between atomistic complexity and mesoscale behavior, ultimately enabling the predictive modeling of nanoporous crystal formation through a computationally tractable methodology.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Boosting Green Hydrogen: Tailored Ni- and Mo-Based Catalysts for Bio-Oil Upgrading through Computational Modeling
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: The valorization of bio-oil into hydrogen via steam reforming presents a sustainable pathway for renewable energy generation. Yet, designing highly active, cost-effective, and stable catalysts for bio-oil steam reforming has always been a challenging pursuit. In this work, we advance the development of two complementary catalyst systems, Ni-based single-atom alloys (SAAs) and MoCoO mixed-metal oxides, each tailored to address key limitations in bio-oil steam reforming. Through density functional theory (DFT) and ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations, we designed and screened bimetallic and trimetallic Ni-based SAA catalysts for acetic acid dehydrogenation, identifying twelve promising compositions based on stability, cost, and resistance to C–C clustering [1]. Notably, Cu–Ni demonstrated superior hydrogen desorption and catalytic performance at 700–1000 K, owing to its favorable surface charge distribution. Trimetallic screening further identified six M1–M2–Ni configurations with balanced hydrogen binding and reduced coking tendencies. In parallel, we investigated Mo-based catalysts for the electrochemical upgrading of biomass-derived furfural, integrating DFT and microkinetic modeling to evaluate activity across Co x MoO y surfaces. Among them, MoCoO₄ exhibited the strongest furfural adsorption, attributed to synergistic interactions between molybdenum and cobalt active sites, which enhance both surface wettability and electron transfer efficiency. These findings support MoCoO₄/activated carbon (AC) as a promising electrocatalyst for producing bio-based chemicals under near-ambient conditions. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Comparative Analysis of One- and Two-Dimensional Membrane Reactor Models: A Case Study on Ammonia Decomposition
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Ammonia is widely recognized by the scientific community as a promising hydrogen carrier due to its high hydrogen content (17.8 wt%), mild liquefaction conditions, and well-established distribution infrastructure [1], [2]. Enhancing the efficiency of ammonia decomposition is a key step toward enabling its application as a hydrogen carrier. Among the various technologies investigated for this purpose, membrane fixed-bed reactors stand out for their capacity to achieve higher conversions while simultaneously producing high-purity hydrogen. While both one- and two-dimensional models for membrane reactors applied to ammonia decomposition have been reported in the literature, a comprehensive comparison between these approaches, particularly in the context of industrial-scale reactors, remains limited. In this study, a multi-tubular membrane fixed-bed reactor for large-scale ammonia decomposition was modeled and simulated using both one-dimensional and two-dimensional approaches. The models were developed based on mass, energy, and momentum conservation equations, using the Aspen Custom Modeler software. Simulations were conducted under varying conditions of space velocity, temperature, and pressure. Additionally, different reactor geometries and catalyst particle sizes were evaluated. The comparison between models enabled the assessment of the impact of radial mass and heat dispersion on ammonia conversion and hydrogen recovery predictions. The two-dimensional model provided detailed insights into radial concentration and temperature gradients within the reactor, highlighting the limitations of the one-dimensional approach under certain operating conditions. The results of this study provide insights for future work on fixed-bed membrane reactor modeling, particularly regarding the selection of model dimensionality. [1] Y. Kojima, “Safety of ammonia as a hydrogen energy carrier,” Int J Hydrogen Energy, vol. 50, pp. 732–739, 2024, doi: 10.1016/j.ijhydene.2023.06.213. [2] H. Ishaq and C. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Bridging Experimental Validation and CFD Modeling for Reactor Scale-up
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: The successful scale-up of chemical reactors remains a critical challenge in chemical engineering, where the prediction of reactor performance relies on the development and validation of kinetic models. Our study exhibits a comprehensive review of the experimental and mathematical modelling approaches for validating kinetic models and explores the role of Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) in reactor scale-up using available literature published over the past 25 years. The present review covers chemical kinetics basics like rate laws, reaction order, and reactor types like batch, continuous stirred tank (CSTR), fluidized bed (FBR), and plug flow reactors. To demonstrate their role in reactor design and optimisation, empirical and mechanistic kinetic modelling approaches are presented. Discussion of mathematical system identification obtained from experimental data includes model development, parameter estimation, and sensitivity analysis. To ensure model robustness and predictive accuracy, structural and numerical identifiability are examined. The recent advances in CFD for reactor scale-up have improved significantly the simulation of hydrodynamics characteristics in chemical reactors by providing crucial information regarding flow patterns, geometry, turbulence modelling, mixing configuration (use of different impeller designs) and residence time distributions, among others. CFD tools enhance and contribute to reactor design and overall process efficiency, ensure uniform distribution of reactants, as well as understand the scale-up impact of operating conditions and prevent or mitigate potential risks. The aim of this comprehensive review is to present and discuss the existing published findings, ongoing research, as well as highlighting and identifying key research gaps and future directions for recommending potential solutions that could lead to substantial innovations and improvement in the fields of Reactor Design and Analysis and Reaction Kinetics. This comprehensive review provides a foundation for improving reactor performance and guiding the mathematical development of more efficient chemical processes, by employing advanced CFD and process simulation tools.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Thermodynamic Evaluation of Mixed Metal Oxides to Minimize Oxygen Carrier Requirements in Autothermal Biomass Chemical Looping Gasification.
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Anthropogenic climate change demands an urgent shift toward sustainable, carbon-neutral solutions. Biomass, a renewable and carbon-neutral resource, presents a viable alternative to fossil fuels for producing high-value chemicals and generating clean energy. However, the low energy density and dispersed availability of biomass necessitate efficient, cost-effective conversion technologies. Chemical looping gasification (CLG) is a promising approach, producing high-purity syngas through redox reactions involving metal oxide oxygen carriers (OCs) in a multi-reactor system. A key challenge in CLG is achieving autothermicity, ensuring that the heat generated in the oxidizer is sufficient to meet the endothermic requirements of biomass gasification in the reducer. As OCs also serve as heat transfer media, high circulation rates are typically required to sustain thermal balance, significantly impacting reactor sizing. One promising solution lies in the use of mixed metal oxide-based OCs, which can lower the endothermic heat requirement of biomass gasification. Although bimetallic systems such as Cu–Fe, Ni–Fe, Mn–Fe, and Co–Fe have been widely studied experimentally, comprehensive system-level thermodynamic analyses to optimize OC composition for reducing OC requirement without compromising syngas quality remain unexplored. This study presents detailed thermodynamic process simulations with a range of mixed metal oxide-based formulations to quantify their effects on system thermodynamics, OC demand, and overall energy efficiency. Notably, incorporating copper into iron-based OCs significantly lowers the endothermic heat requirement, enabling a reduction in OC demand by approximately 30%. Furthermore, steam co-injection is evaluated as a strategy to enhance char conversion and adjust the syngas composition, yielding an H₂/CO ratio of 1.7, ideal for downstream methanol or liquid fuel synthesis. The insights from this work offer a robust framework for the design of mixed metal oxide-based OCs and contribute to the development of efficient, scalable, and economically viable biomass conversion technologies for a sustainable chemical industry.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Coverage Effects of Thiolate Modified Catalysts for Selective Direct Hydrogen Peroxide Synthesis
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Direct synthesis of hydrogen peroxide, involving the reaction of hydrogen and oxygen, offers a promising alternative to the Anthraquinone process due to its milder conditions and the absence of complex, expensive separation steps. However, achieving high selectivity remains a significant challenge, primarily due to the undesired cleavage of the oxygen bond, leading to water formation. This study investigates the use of self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) of thiolates, modifying palladium on alumina, to increase selectivity of the direct synthesis process. Specifically, it first examines how the reduction of active sites affects oxygen dissociation, contributing to water formation. Then it addresses how the interplay between decomposition and hydrogen peroxide synthesis influences overall hydrogen peroxide yields. The study employs HD scrambling to evaluate the relative number of active sites and liquid batch reactions to assess both hydrogen peroxide decomposition and synthesis. The results demonstrate that modified catalysts with relatively high amounts of remaining surface sites accelerate hydrogen peroxide decomposition, lowering the selectivity for hydrogen peroxide production. These findings emphasize the role of available active sites after SAM modification in promoting selective H 2 O 2 production.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: A Scalable Dataset of Organic Reaction Mechanisms Constructed Using Templated-Based Breadth-First Mechanism Intermediate Search
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: The ability to predict the organic reaction mechanism is crucial in many aspects, including reaction condition optimization, methodology optimization, and synthetic route planning. Despite current efforts in leveraging machine learning models to predict reaction mechanisms, the dataset for reaction mechanisms remained scarce. Furthermore, the existing reaction mechanism dataset emphasizes the well-documented reactions, leaving the less-documented reactions underrepresented. In this work, we constructed a new template-based reaction mechanism dataset construction framework. Our approach enumerates all possible mechanisms within a curated set of elementary reaction steps in SMILES Arbitrary Target Specification (SMARTS) to encourage a more explorative reaction mechanism search. We curated 1769 templates from a graduate textbook [1] , and we used these templates to reproduce reaction mechanism pathways for reactions in Pistachio [2] , a database that recorded patented reactions. In total, we reproduced reaction mechanisms for 21,544 reactions with 45,518 mechanistic steps. We subsequently evaluated this dataset by training three different reaction outcome prediction models by conducting mechanism prediction [3][4][5] . The best-performing model achieved 85.50% top-1 accuracy in single-step prediction and 76.88% top-1 accuracy in multistep reaction mechanism prediction. Our model showed capability in exploring less studied reaction mechanisms, which shows our proposed framework an effective solution to explore the ample search space of reaction mechanisms. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Fast Pyrolysis of Bamboo and Polypropylene in a Fluidized Bed Reactor for the Production of High Quality Oil
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Fast pyrolysis was carried out with a mixture of bamboo and PP to research the decomposition characteristics and product distribution. The decomposition of polyolefin-based polymer materials were investigated by analyzing pyrolysis product according to the mixing ratio of bamboo and PP (40~80 wt%) and catalysts. The experiment was carried out using a fluidized bed reactor with a sample size of 0.25–1.70 mm at 450–550 °C for 1 h. Additionally, 100 g of silica sand was used as the bed material, and the nitrogen flow rate was maintained at 2.0ⅹU mf . At 500 °C, the highest bio-oil yield of 79.0 wt% was observed from 80 wt% of PP. Organic fraction in bio-oil was increased in liquid products while increasing PP content, and the selectivity of ethylene (C 3 H 6 ) was increased in gaseous products. As a bed material, 100 g of HZSM-5, Red-mud, and Dolomite with particle sizes of 150 to 212 μm were put into the fluidized bed reactor, and a fast pyrolysis experiment was performed. The liquid yields of HZSM-5, Red-mud, and Dolomite used as catalysts were 63.34 wt%, 68.20 wt%, and 67.44 wt%, respectively, which were lower than sand as bed material, and the moisture content in the liquid product increased. On the other hand, the yield of the gas product more than twice, and the selectivity of hydrogen and methane increased significantly. The calorific value of oil also increased compared to when sand was used. Finally, the compositions of the gas and bio-oil obtained through fast pyrolysis of CM were systematically characterized using GC, GC-MS, 13 C-NMR, calorimeter, and TGA.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Cattesthub: Developing an Experimental Catalytic Database to Promote Rigor and Reproducibility
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: The ability to quantitatively compare newly evolving catalytic materials and technologies is hindered by the widespread availability of catalytic data collected in a consistent manner. While certain catalytic chemistries have been widely studied across decades of scientific research, the ability to quantitatively utilize the available literature information is hindered by variability in reaction conditions, types of reported data, and reporting procedures. Here, we present CatTestHub (www.cpec.umn.edu/cattesthub), a database dedicated to providing benchmarking experimental data for heterogeneous catalysis. Through the selection of probe chemistries, combined with material characterization information and the systematic reporting of kinetic information, the database provides a collection of information that provides a collection of catalytic benchmarks for distinct classes of active sites. We propose that this online and open-access platform could serve as a community wide benchmark, the quality of which is improved through continuous addition of kinetic information on select catalytic systems by members of the heterogeneous catalysis community at large. In this initial iteration, we present benchmarking data relevant to the decomposition of methanol and formic acid over metal surfaces, as well as the Hofmann elimination of alkylamines over aluminosilicate zeolites. Details of the database, the logic of its construction, and the means through which to navigate are presented here, along with examples of catalytic insights readily drawn from the available information. The growth of the database promises to deepen understanding of catalytic behavior, enable modeling based on carefully curated data, and improve the precision of experimental investigations, ultimately expediting the discovery of new, efficient catalytic materials.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Electrochemical Refinery for Sustainable Hydrogen Peroxide Production Using Conducting Polymer and Metal Oxide
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Electrocatalysis offers a promising route to sustainable chemical production by utilizing renewable electricity and abundant precursors like water and oxygen. [1] This work presents an electrochemical refinery (e-refinery) for hydrogen peroxide ( H 2 O 2 ) production, coupling oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) with oxygen evolution reaction (OER). The H 2 O 2 production is achieved through an electrocatalysis-controlled comproportionation reaction. I n the first approach, [2] we adopted conducting polymer, poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):poly(styrene sulfonate) (PEDOT:PSS), as an ORR catalyst to form H 2 O 2 at the cathode. OER over mesoporous nickel oxide (NiO) catalyst was used as auxiliary reaction. This system demonstrates the feasibility of sustainable H 2 O 2 production utilizing only pure water and oxygen feed. The second study explores a platinum group metal (PGM)-free H 2 O 2 electrogenerator employing mesoporous chromium oxide ( Cr 2 O 3 ) for ORR and nickel-cobalt oxide ( NiCo 2 O 4 ) for OER. [3] Cr 2 O 3 showed promising 2e-ORR activity with a H 2 O 2 yield of 70% in alkaline media. Furthermore, the impact of electrolyte flow on the H 2 O 2 electrogenerator's performance was investigated. It shows that one-way feeding of the catholyte can suppress catalyst deterioration and enhance faradaic conversion efficiency. Both studies highlight the potential of PGM-free electrocatalysts in H 2 O 2 electrosynthesis. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Mechanistic Insights into Ethanol Oxidation on n-Type Oxide Supported Gold Catalysts Via Modulation Excitation Spectroscopy and Kinetics
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: This study investigates the role of n-type metal oxide supported gold catalysts in the selective oxidation of ethanol over Au catalysts. We hypothesized that supports enabling charge storage promote O species activation, enhancing selectivity toward acetaldehyde and acetates. Au nanoparticles (~5 nm, 1 wt%) were supported on SrTiO₃ and ZnO and evaluated under identical kinetic conditions (240–270 °C, 5–30 kPa O₂, 0.3–5 kPa ethanol). Ethanol conversion mainly yielded acetaldehyde (80–98%), with minor acetate formation (<10%), following the activity trend: Au/SrTiO₃ > Au/ZnO. Operando frequency-resolved modulation excitation (FR-ME) with DRIFTS and MS identified ethanol and oxygen as positively contributing to acetaldehyde formation. Ethanol modulation correlated with acetaldehyde, water, and acetate signals, while oxygen modulation aligned with acetaldehyde, water, and ethyl acetate, indicating oxygen’s role in promoting oxidation. ME-DRIFTS showed adsorbed ethoxy, acetate, and water species. On Au/SrTiO₃, slow and fast pathways for acetaldehyde formation were observed, along with rapid adsorption/desorption of water and acetate. Au/ZnO exhibited faster charge transfer but limited water dynamics. In situ UV-Vis-NIR via Au-MaPPS showed oxygen adsorption at the Au-support interface and fast charge transfer under reaction conditions. ZnO appeared more reducible, but SrTiO₃ promoted higher activity. Kinetic studies yielded ethanol and O₂ reaction orders of 0.65 and 0.09 for Au/SrTiO₃ (Ea = 57 kJ/mol), and 0.45 and 0.07 for Au/ZnO (Ea = 69 kJ/mol). These results support a Langmuir-Hinshelwood mechanism involving ethanol dissociative adsorption, O₂ activation at the interface, and oxidative dehydrogenation of acetaldehyde as the rate-determining step. Overall, n-type supports enhance activity via charge transfer and O₂ activation, while selectivity is linked to intermediate adsorption and product desorption. Combined modulation excitation spectroscopy and kinetics offer critical insights for designing selective, efficient catalysts.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Structure Sensitivity in CO 2 Methanation over Ni/Al 2 O 3 Catalysts
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: The conversion of CO 2 to methane is a promising strategy for CO 2 utilization, as methane can be integrated into existing natural gas infrastructure for power generation. Nickel (Ni) is an attractive methanation catalyst due to its cost-effectiveness, high availability, and promising activity, despite challenges related to coke formation and sintering. In this work, we investigated the effect of Ni nanoparticle size on Al 2 O 3 -supported catalysts for CO 2 methanation. Ni/Al 2 O 3 catalysts with average particle sizes ranging from 2.8 to 7 nm were synthesized using colloidal synthesis, strong electrostatic adsorption, and incipient wetness impregnation. The particle sizes were characterized using CO chemisorption and TEM/STEM. Methanation reactivity was found to increase with Ni nanoparticle size, correlating with higher H 2 consumption in H 2 -TPR measurements. However, CO 2 -TPD results indicated that reactivity was not directly linked to catalyst basicity. In situ FTIR analysis revealed that only formate species were present on smaller Ni particles under reaction conditions, while both CO and formate species were observed for larger Ni particles. For the most active catalysts with large particles, formyl species on also appeared within the first 10 minutes, alongside CO and formate. We suggest that the changing density of interfacial Ni-Al 2 O 3 sites leads to this observed performance. Figure Caption. FTIR spectra of Ni-based catalysts supported on Al 2 O 3 under CO 2 methanation conditions. All catalysts were reduced in situ at 477 °C for 2 hrs prior to switching to the CO 2 , H 2 , Ar mixture at 300° C. The spectra shown were collected after 10 hrs. of reaction and a background of the reduced catalysts under H 2 /Ar flow is subtracted.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Efficient H 2 O 2 Electrosynthesis Via Amorphous NiO x Nanoparticles on Oxidized Carbon Black
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Two-electron oxygen reduction reaction (2e - ORR) offers a promising route for transforming the synthesis method of H 2 O 2 . An oxidized carbon black based material loaded with amorphous NiO x nanoparticles is proposed as a high-performance 2e - ORR catalyst, which is simply made by an oxidation-impregnation-calcination approach. The catalyst, named as NiO x -C(O)/300°C, offers >90% H 2 O 2 selectivity over a wide potential range with high onset potentials in both alkaline and neutral electrolytic solutions. Moreover, comparative experiments and theoretical calculations confirm the synergistic effect between oxygen functional groups (OFGs) and NiO x particles on the carbon substrate, which indicates that the abundance of carbon-oxygen single bond is crucial for achieving high H 2 O 2 selectivity. This work provides a new insight into the design of carbon-based 2e - ORR catalysts with low-cost transition metal materials.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Transition Metal-Promoted Cu/MgO Catalysts for Enhancing CO 2 Conversion in Reverse Water-Gas Shift (rWGS) Reaction
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: A novel Cu/MgO-based catalyst with transition metals has been developed for the reverse water-gas shift (rWGS) reaction. The rWGS reaction (CO 2 + H 2 ↔ CO + H 2 O, ΔH 0 = 42.1 kJ mol –1 ) is a highly promising reaction for CO 2 utilization with the produced syngas (CO + H 2 ) serving as a key feedstock in C1 chemistry for value-added chemical production via Fischer-Tropsch (F-T) synthesis process. Despite this potential, the endothermic nature of the rWGS reaction necessitates high operating temperatures, limiting its practical applicability. Therefore, developing catalysts that can efficiently convert CO 2 at lower temperatures is essential for sustainable chemical production and CO 2 reduction. Furthermore, catalysts with high selectivity towards CO at low operating pressure can provide strong competitiveness for CO 2 utilization. Herein, the transition metal-promoted Cu/MgO catalyst (Cu/MgO-T) was synthesized with >99.9% CO selectivity. The Cu/MgO-T catalyst exhibited a high CO 2 -to-CO conversion rate of 13% even at low rWGS working temperatures (250℃), close to its theoretical CO 2 -to-CO conversion rate of 16%. Furthermore, this catalyst displayed an unprecedentedly high reaction rate of 216.7 μmol∙g cat –1 ∙s –1 at 400℃. To elucidate the interaction between the transition metal promoter and the Cu/MgO catalyst, several experiments including H 2 -temperature-programmed reduction (H 2 -TPR), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and in-situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier-transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS) were performed. XPS and DRIFTS analyses revealed promoter’s role in the Cu/MgO catalyst, while DRIFTS spectra analysis identified the overall rWGS reaction mechanism and its rate-determining step (RDS) on the Cu/MgO-based catalysts. These findings will provide essential insights for designing optimal catalysts, potentially enhancing the rWGS reaction rate as well as the other CO 2 conversion processes.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Scalable Manufacturing of Inorganic Nanoparticles Using a High-Temperature Jet Mixing Reactor
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Typical laboratory batch reactors for inorganic nanoparticles (NPs) synthesis can be difficult to scale since rapid particle nucleation and growth require efficient mixing to produce monodisperse particle size distribution (PSD). This limits their use in commercial applications. Our work explores a milli fluidic jet mixing reactor (JMR) design consisting of an axial flow with two jets impinging on the mainline, resulting in a single stream that exits the reactor that has mixing time of milliseconds. Our lab has successfully studied the synthesis of metal NPs and core@shell NPs like Pd@TiO2 in JMR at room temperature, where the Pd core was synthesized in batch as it requires high temperature for its formation. The JMR has not been investigated at high temperatures previously resulting in a barrier for a fully continuous nanoparticle synthesis. Keeping in mind the direction of economic feasibility, copper (Cu) was used as a model system to study the behavior of the high-temperature reactor. Preliminary results showed Cu NPs synthesized in JMR have a better PSD than the batch process. Particles synthesized in the batch process were more than 100 nm and agglomerated whereas particles synthesized in high temperature JMR were around 11 nm. The shape and size change of these nanoparticles also changed when the synthesis temperature increased from 100°C to 150°C, at 100°C particles are mostly spherical in batch while at 150°C fractals were seen. In JMR spherical particles were seen at a main line flow rate Q main - 0.8 mL/min and a jet line flow rate of Q jet - 0.4 mL/min whereas nanorods were seen when operated at Q main - 0.4 mL/min, Q jet - 0.2 mL/min. Higher flow rates enhance mixing efficiency, resulting in more uniform reactant distribution and higher supersaturation. Future work will evaluate the yield of Cu NPs in both batch and JMR to address the scalability issues.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Counterion Effects in Deoxydehydration Reactions Catalyzed By Rhenium Salts
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Catalytic deoxydehydration (DODH), which converts vicinal diols into olefins by simultaneously removing one oxygen and water, is one pathway to obtain valuable chemicals and intermediates from biomass-derived sugars or sugar alcohols. Rhenium compounds as simple as perrhenate, ReO 4 - , have been found to be active as soluble or solid catalysts [1]. With the catalytic activity clearly associated with rhenium, the observation of a pronounced counter ion effect is surprising. Prior work is limited [2], and mechanisms generally do not account for this effect, motivating a systematic investigation. Three different perrhenate salts with ammonium, sodium, or potassium as counter ions were compared in liquid-phase batch reactions with 1,2-decanediol as the test reactant and triphenylphosphine as the stoichiometric reductant, at a temperature of 150 °C and autogenous pressure. Product analysis was by GC. One hypothesis was that variable solubility in organic solvents is the cause for differing effectiveness of different rhenium salts, which was sought to be resolved by identifying a suitable solvent and conditions for complete dissolution. Tests of 15 solvents identified the permittivity as giving the best correlations. Solubility of perrhenates increased with increasing solvent relative permittivity ( ε r ) , with >30 required for desired catalyst concentrations of 0.01 M. DODH yields were highest at moderate permittivities (2.20 to 2.40, see figure) and significant only for the ammonium salt. In another approach, dissolution was achieved by adding appropriate amounts of a crown ether. These tests corroborated the inactivity of alkali metal perrhenates. To expand the scope of cations and explore a possible role of acidity, alkali metal perrhenates were tested in the presence of various additives. Ammonium chloride evoked DODH activity, as did alkylammonium chlorides unless they were quaternary. A direct correlation with acidity is unlikely, as similarly acidic boric acid was ineffective, and the effectiveness of methylammonium chlorides increased with increasing substitution.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: A Strategy for the Designing of Nanocatalyst with Single-Cluster Status
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Designing durable and efficient nanocatalysts with single-cluster active sites is a challenging task for these reactions that happened under harsh conditions. Herein, we developed a strategy to prepare a cluster-based nanocatalyst, where the body-centered gold nanocluster (Au 9 ) constructed by nine AU atoms keeps single-cluster status on TiO 2 nanoparticles. This cluster-based catalyst exhibits excellent catalytic performance for the cleave the C-C and C-O bonds and could survive under harsh reaction conditions. https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: A Global Kinetic Model for High Temperature Homogeneous Oxidative Dehydrogenation of Ethane
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Ethylene is an indispensable chemical commodity to produce a variety of important products including polyethylene, ethylene oxide, vinyl chloride and various others. Steam cracking is being employed in the industry to produce ethylene and being of endothermic nature, it requires elevated temperature input typically 800-900 deg C (tube temperature can rise to 1100 deg C). This high temperature requirement can adversely affect the life of reactor tubes and require periodic shutdown for coke removal. Oxidative Dehydrogenation of Ethane (ODHE) has surfaced as a potential alternative. Several catalysts have been reported in the literature; however, little work has been presented in the past incorporating homogenous chemistry which can be an emergent competing alternative. Considering promising performance, it makes things holistically viable by reducing the overall complexity of modelling followed by process scale-up. The influence of homogeneous chemistry plays a pivotal role even with a catalytic system when high temperature operation is anticipated and may stand out under certain process conditions; therefore, it is utmost necessary to corroborate such behavior independently. For the kinetic model perspective, previous studies were mainly focused on micro-kinetics comprising of several species and reaction steps. The present work focuses on presenting seven-reactions/eight-species based global kinetic model for high temperature homogeneous oxidative dehydrogenation of ethane. Model predictions are compared with available literature data as well as obtained experimental data to validate the approach as well as the kinetic constants to determine ethane and oxygen conversion, product distribution profile in terms of selectivity and ethylene yield under various feed ratios, space time and temperature conditions. Thermodynamics and effect of different characteristic time scales in ascertaining isothermal and adiabatic conditions in a laboratory scale tubular reactor and to briefly elucidate reaction pathway assessment, product co-feed experiments, influence of cracking chemistry and overall modeling approach are also elucidated in the study.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Computational Design of Mercury Oxidation Catalysts: From Support Modifications to Active Site Design
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Mercury (Hg) emissions from fossil fuel combustion facilities pose a significant threat to the global environment due to their high toxicity and bioaccumulation potential. Catalytic oxidation of elemental Hg using heterogeneous metal oxide catalysts has emerged as an economically and catalytically efficient approach for Hg removal. In this study, we present a comprehensive investigation of mercury oxidation catalysts using an integrated computational approach combining density functional theory (DFT) calculations and advanced machine learning methodologies. We first examined how modifications to the TiO₂ support structure (crystallographic phase control and reduction treatment) affect the Hg oxidation activity of VO x /TiO₂ catalysts. We found that phase control from anatase to rutile enhanced the Hg oxidation activity, while reduction treatment decreased it due to changes in the charge density at the VO x active center. Notably, the interaction between the V site and surface Cl played a critical role in balancing two key reaction steps of HCl dissociation and HgCl₂ desorption. Then, we systematically investigated various transition metal oxide clusters (MnO₂, Fe₂O₃, CuO, CoO, MoO₃, and CeO₂) supported on TiO₂ as alternative catalysts for low-temperature mercury oxidation. For the HgCl₂ formation pathway, CeO₂/TiO₂ demonstrated superior performance, while CuO/TiO₂ exhibited enhanced activity in the HgO formation pathway. Through various electronic structure analyses, we identified key electronic descriptors for catalytic activity, including charge density of active metal centers, Fermi level position, and metal-oxygen bond strength. Throughout these studies, the relationship between electronic structure and catalytic activity was interpreted within the Sabatier principle, confirming that optimal catalytic activity requires moderate interaction strength between reactants and catalysts. These findings provide molecular-level understanding for the rational design of mercury oxidation catalysts and offer valuable guidelines for developing technologies for mercury emission control and multi-pollutant removal systems.

The basic nature of the support has led to enhanced carbon dioxide, a prime component of biogas, adsorption and conversion in the millisecond reactor.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Improved Durability of Ni/YSZ-Based Catalysts for Ammonia Cracking in Solid Oxide Fuel Cells
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Ammonia (NH 3 ) has emerged as a promising hydrogen carrier due to its high gravimetric and volumetric hydrogen storage capacities, along with its carbon-free nature. Its direct utilization in solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) offers an attractive route for sustainable power generation. However, the development of robust anode catalysts for direct ammonia-fed SOFCs remains a significant challenge, particularly due to performance degradation at high operating temperatures (700–900 °C), especially under thermal cycling. One major degradation mechanism is believed to be of the anode material, which not only reduce catalytic activity but also compromise mechanical stability. In this study, we report on an enhanced Ni/YSZ-based anode catalyst with improved resistance to sintering and nitridation during ammonia decomposition at temperatures above 600 °C. The impact of surface treatment strategies on catalyst durability is also evaluated and discussed.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Reverse Microemulsion Synthesis As an Efficient Method for Synthesis of Highly Active Catalytic Nanomaterials for CO 2 Conversion to Renewable Synthetic Fuels
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: In a reverse microemulsion (RME), water nano-droplets are surrounded by surfactant molecules and dispersed in a continuous oil phase. RMEs are clear, thermodynamically stable isotropic mixtures that form by self-assembly upon mixing. Water nanodroplets can contain reactants. If two (or more) RMEs containing different reactants are mixed, the reaction happens when nanodroplets collide and merge, resulting in a gradual process of nanoparticles self-assembly. The nanoparticles are extracted by changing the RME composition, disrupting the thermodynamic stability. Upon segregation of aqueous and organic phases, nanoparticles undergo aggregation within the aqueous phase, followed by sedimentation. Various catalytic nanomaterials were synthesized using Al 2 O 3 and CeO 2 as supports and Cu, Fe, Co, Ni and Mo as active phases (as metal oxide or carbide). Resulted SSAs ranged from 200-400 m 2 /g and the nanoparticle size was less than 20 nm. The catalysts were characterized by ICP-OES, XPS, XRD, BET, and TEM to investigate chemical composition, crystallinity, and morphology. TPR and TPD were employed to investigate reducibility and adsorption properties, and in situ FTIR was used to investigate the surface reactivity. Reaction tests were conducted in a continuous flow reactor in a wide range of operating conditions such as temperature, pressure and flow rate. The outlet from the reactor was analyzed via IR and FTIR and GC. The catalysts exhibited different levels of catalytic activity and selectivity, ranging from CO and CH 4 to light hydrocarbons as products. For certain materials, CO 2 conversions approached the chemical equilibrium level (e.g., 95% CO 2 conversion and 100% selectivity). Catalyst stability was also investigated comprehensively. The results of catalytic perfomance evaluation were correlated with the results of materials characterization, while focusing on the structure-property relationship. Our work provides an avenue for developing highly efficient materials for CO 2 conversion to renewable fuels, while also providing fundamental insights into the structure-activity relationship.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: The Influence of Nickel Dispersion and Alumina Structure on the Ammonia Decomposition
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: Hydrogen is a key alternative to fossil fuels due to its zero CO₂ emissions, but challenges in transportation limit its widespread use. Ammonia is considered a promising hydrogen carrier. Various catalysts have been studied for this process, with nickel-based catalysts standing out among non-noble metals for their low cost and favorable catalytic properties. This study focuses on investigating nickel catalysts supported on different alumina types, emphasizing how the support material impacts metal dispersion in ammonia decomposition. Different alumina was employed in 𝛾-Al 2 O 3 , θ-Al 2 O 3 , and α-Al 2 O 3 . Nickel was impregnated (10%) on the alumina supports and calcined at 450 °C. Catalyst characterizations using specific surface area (S BET ), CO chemisorption, X-ray diffraction (XRD), and temperature-programmed reduction (H 2 -TPR). Catalytic tests were carried out at temperature range of 300 to 650°C with pure NH₃. These results of XRD patterns (Figure 1) confirm the successful incorporation of nickel onto the Al₂O₃ supports. The H 2 -TPR profile (Figure 2) of Ni-based catalysts supported on alumina is characterized by three distinct peaks: α, β, and γ. These peaks correspond to the reduction of Ni species with varying metal-support interactions. The activity and reaction rate of ammonia decomposition of all catalysts a dependence on temperature (Figure 3). The 10Ni/𝛾-Al 2 O 3 catalyst exhibited the highest conversion (95%) at 550 °C, which that the 10Ni/θ-Al 2 O 3 follows with a conversion of 88.8% and 10Ni/α-Al 2 O 3 of 86.3%. These results indicate that the alumina structure of did not influence the Ni particle dispersion on consequently the activity (Table 1). The hydrogen rate production increases with temperature (Figure 3), reaching maximum rates of 60.50 mmol min -1 g -1 for 100% ammonia conversion at 600 °C. In conclusion, the catalytic performance of the activity and rate production were independent of the alumina structure and the Ni particle sizes. However, the performances depend solely on the temperature.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Tuning Nanoparticle Proximity and Size: Controlling the Agglomeration Narrative of Metal/TiO 2 Nanosheet Catalytic Systems
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: The design of metal oxide (MO x ) supported metal nanoparticles (NP) as heterogeneous catalysts has garnered significant attention. However, the sintering of supported metal NPs has been a perennial challenge. This requires careful consideration for the choice of MO x support such as titania and modulating the physical attributes (example: size, proximity, dispersity) of NPs on the support. Here, we have developed a better synthetic protocol to fabricate Cu/TiO 2 and Fe/TiO 2 catalysts by tweaking the pathways of NP deposition. To modulate the proximity and size of nanoparticles, the synthetic protocol involves changing the physical parameters of the mother liquor, such as pH and the addition of organic ligand. The Fe and Cu NPs were successfully deposited on the titania surface, as shown in Figure 1. We have obtained a size range of 1.5-4 nm and proximity in the range of 6-12 nm for Fe NPs by varying the pH of the mother liquor. The increase in particle size and proximity is inversely proportional to the solution's pH. Further, homogeneity in the dispersion of NPs on the titania support was then modulated by the addition of a suitable amine ligand during synthesis. The standard deviation for the proximity of Fe NPs on TiO 2 was calculated to be 2.87 nm for the modified protocol (Fe/TiO 2 _M) (Figure 1 F) against the standard deviation of 3.37 nm for Fe NPs on TiO 2 NS in case of unmodified protocol (Fe/TiO 2 _U) (Figure 1 E). A comparable increase in the oxygen vacancies on the TiO 2 nanosheet surface was observed in the O1s spectrum of the XPS analysis data, in case of modified TiO 2 support which supports the enhanced Fe deposition TiO 2 NS. In summary, this investigation helps establish control over the size, proximity, and distribution of metal on TiO 2 systems which is key to increase their effective catalytic lifetime.

https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.title: Molecular Structure of Na-WO x /SiO₂ Catalysts Under Operating Conditions: Dispersed Vs. Crystalline Phases in Selective Methane Activation during OCM
https://aiche.confex.com/aiche/2025/meet.abstract: The oxidative coupling of methane (OCM) offers a direct route to produce valuable C₂ hydrocarbons, yet the underlying catalytic mechanisms remain elusive. The Mn₂O₃-Na₂WO₄/SiO₂ system has demonstrated high activity (~30% CH₄ conversion) and selectivity (~70% C₂), but the molecular origin of active sites governing methane activation and selectivity is not well understood. This study explores the fundamental surface chemistry of Na-WOx/SiO₂ catalysts, focusing on how dispersed and crystalline Na-WOx phases influence catalytic performance. We hypothesize that dispersed Na-WOx sites selectively activate methane by forming reactive atomic oxygen species (O*), facilitating C₂H₆ formation while mitigating overoxidation. In contrast, crystalline Na₂WO₄ structures transition into a molten phase under reaction conditions, promoting molecular oxygen species (O₂*), which drive unselective oxidation pathways. To probe these effects, we systematically synthesized Na-WOx/SiO₂ catalysts via incipient wetness impregnation, enabling precise control over the ratio of dispersed Na-WOx and crystalline Na₂WO₄. In situ Raman spectroscopy elucidated molecular structures, linking surface phase composition to catalytic function measured using high resolution photoionization mass spectroscopy (PIMS) while near ambient XPS provided insights into surface elemental changes. Our findings provide fundamental insights into reaction kinetics and active site behavior in OCM, offering a rational design approach for more selective and efficient catalysts.
